items.k: The TAG method | Term | Anchor | Glue | See the difference | Weak | Strong
items.x: How to answer The TAG method Use these three moves, in this order, every time. T Term State the term precisely in your first sentence. Do not ease into it with a story or a general opener like "In psychology, many things affect behaviour". A Anchor Name your example straight after the term: a study or a realistic situation. G Glue Write the sentence that connects them: "This demonstrates [term] because [how it works here]." This sentence is the exact difference between a 3 and a 4. See the difference Weak Schema theory is when people use prior knowledge to understand things. Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study is an example. Strong Schema theory proposes that prior knowledge is organised into mental frameworks that shape and can distort recall. Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study demonstrates this because participants recalling an unfamiliar story changed unfamiliar details to fit story structures familiar from their own culture, showing that memory is reconstructive rather than an exact copy. The weak version names an example. The strong version explains the term and says what in the example shows it.

Notice that the command term is explain , so you need a reason or cause, not just a definition. Move What it sounds like Term Anchoring bias is a cognitive bias in which people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they receive (the anchor) when making a judgement, and then adjust away from it too little. Anchor For example, a shopper in a Dubai mall sees a jacket labelled "Was AED 600, now AED 299". Glue This demonstrates anchoring bias because the first number, AED 600, becomes the reference point for judging value. Using fast, effortless System 1 thinking, and with little time or information to compare prices elsewhere, the shopper judges AED 299 against the anchor instead of against what similar jackets usually cost, so it feels like a bargain even if it is the normal price. The marks are for application: how well you make the theory explain this situation. items.x: The markband How Section B is marked Marks What your answer looks like 1 to 2 Limited knowledge, and only a thin link to the scenario. items.t: Section B: applying to an unseen scenario
items.k: The CLUE method | Call out the concept | Locate the evidence | Unpack the mechanism | Echo back to the scenario | The cover test
items.x: How to answer The CLUE method C Call out the concept Name the theory or term in your very first sentence, with a brief, accurate explanation. L Locate the evidence Point to the exact detail in the scenario that signals it. Paraphrase it briefly. Do not copy the scenario out. U Unpack the mechanism Explain, step by step, how and why that detail produces the behaviour, using accurate terminology. E Echo back to the scenario Close by tying the mechanism back to the named people or setting. Connect it; do not just retell the story. The cover test Cover the scenario with your hand. Does your answer still make complete sense without it? If yes, you have written a Section A-style definition, not a Section B application. Go back and name the specific details you are explaining.

The head of year introduces a new system: every week that a class submits at least 90% of its homework on time, the whole class earns 15 minutes of free reading or board games on Thursday afternoon. After six weeks, late submissions have fallen sharply. During the exam period the reward is paused, and late submissions begin to rise again. Explain how operant conditioning could explain the change in the students' behaviour. [6] Try planning it yourself first, then reveal the plan. Show all answers Tap a blurred cell to reveal it. Move Plan C Operant conditioning is learning in which the consequence of a behaviour changes how likely it is to be repeated. A pleasant consequence that strengthens a behaviour is positive reinforcement. L The free time on Thursday only happens if the class submits at least 90% of homework on time. Late submissions fell over six weeks, then rose when the reward was paused. U The free time is a positive reinforcer that depends on the behaviour, so students learn that on-time submission

items.s: Two shapes to be ready for
items.k: Two shapes to be ready for | 1. "With reference to this study, explain..." | 2. "Explain how [theory] could be used to..."
items.x: Question shapes Two shapes to be ready for 1. "With reference to this study, explain..." You get a study and a model or theory. Use the study as evidence: say which parts of the model it supports, and which parts it does not actually test. In the specimen paper's imagination study, children were seen selecting and combining toy parts, which supports the stages of the model. But the model says the combining is random , and the study never tests that. Spotting what a study does not show is application too. 2. "Explain how [theory] could be used to..." You are asked to suggest a strategy, often for a school or community. Choose one realistic strategy and link each part of it to a specific part of the theory. For social learning theory, a peer-mentor programme works well because you can link each step to attention, retention, reproduction and motivation, and to identification with a model students admire.

items.k: Evaluate, discuss, to what extent | Evaluate | Discuss | To what extent | The shared trap
items.x: Command terms Evaluate, discuss, to what extent Evaluate Weigh strengths against limitations. You need at least one real strength, at least one real limitation, and an explicit act of weighing them to reach a judgement. Two lists are not an evaluation. Discuss A balanced review of a range of arguments or factors, ending in a clear conclusion that the rest of the essay supports. To what extent Test a claim. The answer is not yes or no but a position on a scale (largely, partly, minimally), stated early so the examiner knows where you are heading. The shared trap All three fail in the same way: the content is described accurately but never weighed or judged. The jump from 7 to 9 up to 10 to 12 is not more content. items.x: The six concepts Use the concept as a lens, not a label The same concept looks different depending on the area of study, but the questions you ask with it stay the same. Use the trigger questions to get your thinking started. Concept Core idea Trigger questions A shallow use to avoid Bias Behaviour, theories and research are shaped by systematic distortions in who is studied, how findings are interpreted and which explanation is favoured. Who produced this finding, and what might have skewed it? Whose perspective is missing? Is the theory one-sided? Naming "sampling bias" without saying how it narrows the conclusion. Causality Behaviour rarely has one cause. Much research is correlational, and correlations are often mistaken for causes. Is this cause and effect, or an association? Could the direction be reversed? Could a third variable explain both? "Correlation is not causation" as a slogan, without applying it. Change Behaviour changes gradually or suddenly, by choice or by forces outside our control. items.k: Experiment
items.x: Experiment Learning and cognition Aim To investigate whether a 30-second wait before recall affects how many words people remember, compared with recalling immediately. Method Experiment with two conditions. Independent samples: each participant was in one group only. Minimum sample For a student-led experiment the guide sets at least five participants with repeated measures, or ten with independent samples. This design used independent samples, so ten is the minimum. IV Whether recall came after a 30-second wait or straight away. DV Number of words correctly recalled out of 20, written down. Procedure Both groups saw the same list of 20 words. One group wrote down what they remembered immediately. The other waited 30 seconds first. Scores were counted and compared. Data Quantitative: a score out of 20 for each participant. Ethics Informed consent, right to withdraw, debrief, anonymised scores. Low risk of harm. Watch out There was no task during the wait, so people could rehearse the words. The wait and the word display were not timed exactly. Both weaken internal validity. From your notes Sampling technique, group sizes, how participants were put into groups.

items.k: Observation
items.x: Observation Human development Aim To investigate how people use devices in everyday settings. Method Naturalistic, non-participant, structured observation, at home or in a public cafe. At home it was overt (the family gave permission); in the cafe it was covert (people were not told). Non-participant means the observer did not join in. Recorded In each 15-minute block: the number of uses (pick-ups), the total duration of use, and an approximate age band. Data Quantitative: counts and durations, grouped by age band. Ethics At home, adults in the family gave permission in advance. In the cafe, consent was not asked: covert observation is acceptable only in a public place where people expect to be seen by strangers. Privacy protected: no names, no images, age bands only. A teacher approved the plan, and students observing in public went with an adult. Watch out One observer judging what counts as one use. Ages are estimates. Who happens to be in the setting is not controlled. No IV, so patterns only, not causes. items.k: Interview
items.x: Interview Health and well-being Aim To investigate how Grade 12 students describe coping with the stress of university applications. Method Semi-structured interview: an opening, a set of core questions, and follow-up questions that depend on the answers. Participants Grade 12 students (DP or AP) who are applying to university now and do not take psychology. Purposive sample: they have the experience the aim is about. It also has features of an opportunity sample, because we interviewed those who were available and agreed. Recording Audio recorded with permission, transcribed, and the transcript checked against the recording. Analysis Two stages. First, inductive content analysis: themes came from the transcripts themselves. Second, deductive coding: each coping response was coded as problem-focused or emotion-focused, using Lazarus and Folkman's framework. Data Qualitative: the participants' own words. Ethics Consent to take part and to recording, right to withdraw, a code instead of a name, recording deleted within 7 days, debrief. Watch out Leading questions, social desirability (wanting to look organised or calm), interviewer effects, and judgement when coding. From your notes

Method A questionnaire on a Google Form. Cross-sectional: two existing groups, Grade 11 and Grade 12, compared at one point in time. Grade was not manipulated, so this is not an experiment. Participants Each of us surveyed one Grade 11 and one Grade 12 student who was 16 or older, did not take psychology and was not in our class: about 34 participants (the guide minimum for a survey is 10). items.x: Concepts Meaning, what it looks like, and the trap The first four come up most often. Change and perspective are less common on Paper 2, but they can still be asked. Concept Meaning In research it looks like Not this Bias A limitation in objective thinking: a filter of experience or preference that distorts how data are collected or read. Researcher bias, participant bias such as social desirability, sampling bias, confirmation bias. Any mistake at all. Causality Whether a change in one variable produces a change in another. Only a method that manipulates an IV and controls other variables can test cause and effect. Two things happening together (that is correlation). Measurement How a behaviour is operationalised so it can be recorded reliably and represented validly. Counts and scores, or transcripts and codes. Qualitative data are measured too. Generalisability. Responsibility The researcher's ethical duties to participants and to how findings are used. Consent, withdrawal, anonymity, debrief. These can change who takes part and what they say. The participant's responsibility. Change Whether, and how, a study can show behaviour shifting over time or after an intervention.

items.x: Section B [15] Discuss an unseen study through the concepts You get a short description of a study you have never seen. It may be experimental or non-experimental, and it is set in one of the four contexts. The question lists four or more concepts and asks you to discuss the study with reference to two or more of them. The specimen question reads: "Discuss the following study with reference to two or more of the following concepts: bias, causality, measurement, and/or responsibility. [15]" Two concepts can be enough You can go deep on two concepts or wider with three. Both are accepted. Two well-developed concepts usually beat four thin ones.

items.x: Practice A practice study Fictional study, written for practice. Context: human relationships Researchers at a university in the UAE wanted to find out whether students change their opinions to match a group, and whether this depends on how strongly the students identify with that group. They invited 96 first-year undergraduates (all studying psychology, aged 18 to 20, 71% female) to take part in return for course credit. Before the main task, all participants completed a six-item questionnaire in which they rated statements such as "I am proud to be a student of this university" from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Scores were added to give an identification score from 6 to 30. Participants were then told that they would join an online group chat with four other students from their university and rate 12 posters for a campus festival from 1 (poor) to 10 (excellent). In reality, the other four "students" were computer-controlled accounts. Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the majority condition, the four accounts posted their ratings first, and these were always at least 3 points lower than the average rating the same poster had received

items.x: Toolkit Words you need for every Paper 3 Quantitative sources Mean, median, mode : the typical score. The median resists outliers. Standard deviation, range, semi-interquartile range : how spread out scores are. The semi-interquartile range is half the distance between the lower and upper quartiles; like the median, it resists outliers. Overlap : if two groups' spreads overlap a lot, a gap in means matters less. Skew : a long tail on one side pulls the mean towards it. Correlation (r) : direction and strength, never cause. Significance : the result is unlikely to be due to chance (p < 0.05). With a critical value table, check the test's rule: for most tests the calculated value must be larger than the critical value, but for Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon T it must be smaller. Effect size : how big the difference is, not just whether it is real. Named tests : tests of difference (chi-square, related and unrelated t-tests, Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon T) and tests of relationship (correlation coefficients). You read and interpret a reported result; you never calculate one. Qualitative sources Credibility : do the findings truly reflect the participants' experiences? Bias : did the

items.s: One issue that limits how we can read the data
items.k: The examiner lesson | interpreting the data as shown
items.x: What Q1 asks One issue that limits how we can read the data Source 1 is printed on the question paper, usually as a graph or table. Q1 asks you to explain one thing about how the data is presented or summarised that stops us reading it with confidence. The examiner lesson Q1 is about interpreting the data as shown , not about the study's validity. In the IB-marked samples, explaining a shortened y-axis earned full marks. Listing general validity issues such as sample size or demand characteristics does not answer the question unless you show how it limits reading the graph or table itself. Mark What it takes (paraphrased from the guide) 1 You name a relevant issue. 2 You describe it clearly, pointing to where it is in the source. 3 You explain it: what a reader might wrongly conclude, and why.

items.k: Identify, point, explain | Identify | Point | Explain | Frame | Only one
items.x: The structure Identify, point, explain 1 Identify Name the issue in one phrase: "The y-axis starts at 40, not 0." 2 Point Use the actual values from the source: "so the bars for 46 and 48 look very different." 3 Explain Say what a reader would wrongly conclude: "This exaggerates a 2-point difference, so we cannot judge how meaningful it is." Frame: "One issue is that . In source 1, (quote values or labels). This limits interpretation because a reader might conclude , when in fact ." Only one The question asks for one issue, and only the first issue you write is marked, even if a later one is better. Writing three short ones does not earn more than one well-explained one. Lead with the clearest and develop it.

items.s: What to look for in source 1
items.k: What to look for in source 1
items.x: The issue menu What to look for in source 1 Look at Issue Why it limits interpretation The y-axis Starts above zero (truncated) Small differences look large. Axis labels and units Missing, vague ("Score"), or scale not explained We cannot tell what was measured or whether high is good or bad. Categories Groups or labels that are not defined, such as "healthy" and "unhealthy" use We cannot tell what was counted in each group, so the same graph could mean different things to different readers. Spread Means with no SD, range or error bars We cannot tell whether groups overlap, so a small gap may mean nothing. The x-axis Unequal time intervals or bin widths drawn evenly Trends look steeper or flatter than they are; distributions look a different shape. Rates Rates without a base (per 100 or per 1,000?) Groups cannot be compared fairly. Two y-axes Different scales on left and right Lines can be made to cross or match by choosing the scales. Percentages Do not add to 100, or categories overlap We cannot tell how many people chose each option or whether people were counted twice. The title Causal wording ("X improves Y") on correlational data Invites a cause-and-effect reading the data

items.k: Analyse, then conclude | The examiner lesson | overlap | skew
items.x: What Q2 asks Analyse, then conclude "Analyse" means break the findings down to bring out what matters. Q2 has two jobs: a detailed analysis of the numbers in source 2, and a conclusion that is explicitly linked to those findings and to the claim. Marks Analysis Conclusion 1 to 2 Limited, or contains mistakes. Attempted but not relevant. 3 to 4 Accurate but lacks detail or development. Stated, but the link to the findings is unclear. 5 to 6 The data is analysed in detail. Explicitly linked to the findings. Paraphrased from the guide's Q2 markband. The examiner lesson In the IB-marked samples, responses lost marks for not mentioning the overlap or the skew of the data, and for a conclusion that was "very general". One response also went beyond the data, which is never rewarded.

items.k: Five analysis moves | Check the direction of the test | larger | smaller
items.x: The moves Five analysis moves You will rarely need all five. Use every one the data allows. Move What you write 1. Compare the centres "The online group's mean (12.4) was 1.1 points lower than the face-to-face group's (13.5)." 2. Compare the spread "But the online group was more varied (SD 4.8 vs 2.9), so the mean hides a wide range of outcomes." 3. Look at overlap and shape "The interquartile ranges overlap almost completely. The online group is positively skewed: a few high scores pull its mean up." 4. Check significance "The calculated U of 41 is above the critical value of 37, so the difference is not significant at p < 0.05." 5. Note what the data cannot tell us "Only 18 participants were in each group, and the study did not include a follow-up, so we cannot judge whether the effect lasted." Check the direction of the test For most tests (t, chi-squared, z) the result is significant when the calculated value is larger than the critical value. For Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon T it must be smaller . Read what the source says before you decide.

Bias Researcher's role or relationship with participants (teacher, manager, clinician); leading questions; group setting; sensitive topic; researcher knew the hypothesis; self-selected sample. items.x: Points of view What counts as a point of view A point of view is a position someone could reasonably take on the claim. items.x: Structure A plan that works in 45 minutes Part What goes in it Time Introduction Restate the claim, define its key terms, give your position in one sentence ("The claim is supported for X, but not for Y"). 4 min Supporting evidence The strongest source for the claim: what it shows (with a number), why it supports the claim, how far we can trust it. Link a theory from your own knowledge. 10 min Challenging evidence The strongest source against the claim, treated the same way. 10 min Complicating evidence A source showing it depends: on who, what kind, how much. This is usually where top answers earn their marks. 10 min Evaluation of the points of view Weigh the sides: design, sample, triangulation. Which way does the balance of evidence fall? 6 min Conclusion Answer "to what extent" directly, with the conditions under which the claim holds. 5 min Source sentence: "Source (a with participants in ) found . This supports / challenges the claim because . However, (limitation), so ." Evaluating points of view: "Although source suggests , source is stronger evidence because . Taken together, the sources suggest that ."

items.x: Own knowledge Bring in what you know, briefly and relevantly Own knowledge is anything not in the booklet: theories, concepts and studies about the HL extension and the context. Use it to explain why a source found what it did, or to show that a pattern holds or fails elsewhere. One or two sentences per idea is usually enough. Culture Cultural dimensions (individualism and collectivism), independent and interdependent self, emic and etic approaches, imposed etic, WEIRD samples, acculturation strategies. Motivation Self-determination theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness), intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, overjustification effect, goal-setting, expectancy and self-efficacy. Technology Displacement hypothesis, the "Goldilocks" idea of moderate use, cognitive load and multitasking, cognitive offloading, active versus passive use, digital divide. Do not write a Paper 1 essay Own knowledge supports your interpretation of the sources. If a paragraph never mentions a source, it is probably drifting.

items.x: Learning as a change in behaviour In psychology, learning is a relatively lasting change in behaviour that comes from experience. Growing taller is not learning; fastening your seatbelt without thinking, after hundreds of car journeys, is. In the early twentieth century, a group of psychologists called behaviourists argued that psychology should study only what can be observed: stimuli in the environment and the responses people and animals make to them. John B. Watson was one of the first to make this argument. Behaviourists studied two kinds of learning by association, called conditioning . Classical conditioning : learning that two stimuli go together. It works on automatic responses,

items.k: Classical conditioning: learning by association | Unconditioned stimulus (UCS | Unconditioned response (UCR | Neutral stimulus (NS | Conditioned stimulus (CS | Conditioned response (CR
items.x: Classical conditioning: learning by association Classical conditioning Ivan Pavlov was a Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his research on digestion. While he was measuring how much saliva dogs produced, he noticed that they began to salivate before the food arrived. This led him to study how a new stimulus could come to trigger a reflex. He trained hungry dogs to salivate at the sound of a metronome or a buzzer that had been repeatedly presented just before food. Classical conditioning has five key terms. Learn them in this order. Unconditioned stimulus (UCS): something that triggers a response naturally, with no learning. For Pavlov's dogs, the food. Unconditioned

items.x: Operant conditioning: learning from consequences Operant conditioning Edward Thorndike (1898) placed hungry cats in a puzzle box, a crate with a latch or loop that opened the door. Food was outside the box. At first the cats moved about at random. When a random movement opened the door, they escaped and reached the food. Over repeated trials, the time they took to escape fell gradually. Thorndike explained this with the law of effect : behaviour that is followed by a satisfying consequence becomes more likely to happen again in that situation, and behaviour that is followed by an unpleasant consequence becomes less likely. B. F. Skinner (1938) developed this idea into operant conditioning .

items.x: Schedules of reinforcement and shaping How often reinforcement arrives changes the pattern of behaviour. Continuous reinforcement (a reward every time) produces fast learning, but the behaviour also stops quickly once the reward stops. Partial reinforcement (a reward only some of the time) is slower to build, but the behaviour lasts longer when rewards stop. Skinner described four partial schedules. items.x: Learning by watching Social learning theory Social learning theory (SLT) proposes that people learn by watching other people, not only by doing things themselves and being rewarded or punished. Albert Bandura developed the theory from the 1960s onwards. Learning by watching is called observational learning . The person who is watched is the model . Modelling is the process of showing a behaviour that someone else can observe and copy. When the observer copies it, we call this imitation . Models can be live , such as a parent, a teacher or an older cousin, or symbolic , such as a person in a film or a video. People learn skills, habits, emotional reactions and attitudes this way. items.x: Identification: who do we copy? We do not copy everyone we see. Identification is when an observer feels similar to a model, or wants to be like them, and so is more likely to adopt the model's behaviour. SLT predicts that people are more likely to imitate a model who: is similar to them, for example the same sex or a similar age; has high status or seems competent, such as a team captain or a respected teacher; is seen being rewarded for the behaviour. items.x: What is a schema? Schema theory A schema (plural: schemas or schemata) is a mental framework of knowledge about something: an object, a place, an event, a group of people, or yourself. Schemas are built from past experience and stored in long-term memory. Your schema for a classroom includes desks, a board, a teacher, other students and the rule that you put your hand up to speak. You do not have to think about any of this. Schema theory is a cognitive model. It proposes that what we already know shapes how we take in, store, remember and act on new information. items.x: How schemas change: assimilation and accommodation Schemas are not fixed. The terms used to describe how they change come from Piaget, who studied how children's thinking develops. Assimilation happens when new information fits an existing schema, so it is added without changing the schema. A young child with a schema for "bird" (feathers, wings, flies) sees a falcon for the first time and recognises it as a bird. The schema stays the same. Accommodation happens when new information does not fit, so the schema has to be changed or a new one created. The same child sees a bat and calls it a bird, because it has wings and flies. items.x: Two ways of thinking Dual processing theory The dual processing theory proposes that people think in two different ways. System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless. Some researchers prefer to talk about Type 1 and Type 2 processes, to avoid suggesting that there are two separate parts of the brain. items.x: What is a cognitive bias? A cognitive bias is a systematic error in thinking. "Systematic" means the error is not random: it pushes many people's judgements in the same direction, in the same kinds of situation. In the warm-up, the first number was only a question, yet it is likely that the Version B group gave higher estimates than the Version A group. That pattern is a bias. items.x: Anchoring bias Anchoring bias Anchoring bias is the tendency for an initial value (the anchor) to pull a later numerical judgement towards it. People start from the anchor and adjust, but the adjustment is usually too small, so the final answer stays close to where they started. Anchors can be relevant or irrelevant. A relevant anchor is a number that should matter, such as the original price of a phone. An irrelevant anchor has no logical link to the answer, such as a number on a spinning wheel. items.x: Debiasing: can we reduce cognitive biases? Debiasing strategies try to reduce the effect of a cognitive bias on a decision. Most of them work by getting System 2 to check what System 1 has offered. Telling people that a bias exists is usually not enough, because they do not notice the bias happening in their own thinking. Common strategies include: Consider the opposite. Before deciding, list reasons why the anchor, or your current belief, might be wrong. Slow down. Build in a pause or a checklist before important decisions, so a quick answer is not accepted automatically. Look for disconfirming evidence. Anchoring has appeared with students, car experts and legal professionals, which suggests it is a general feature of human thinking. items.x: What is a cognitive model? Cognitive models Nobody can open a skull and see a memory. What psychologists can see is behaviour: how many words a person recalls, which words they recall, and how quickly they answer. A cognitive model is a simplified description of a mental process that explains this behaviour. It is usually drawn as boxes (parts of the system, such as a store) and arrows (how information moves between them). A cognitive model is not a map of the brain. items.x: The multi-store model (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968) The multi-store model (MSM) proposes that memory is made of three separate stores. Information flows through them in a fixed order. Sensory memory. Everything you see, hear and touch enters sensory memory first. It holds a lot of information, but only for a very short time (less than a second for visual information). Only information you pay attention to moves on. Short-term memory (STM). STM holds the information you are aware of right now. items.k: Problems with the multi-store model | STM may not be one store | Rehearsal is not the only route into LTM | STM does more than store
items.x: Problems with the multi-store model STM may not be one store. Shallice and Warrington (1970) described patient KF, who had brain damage after a motorcycle accident. His short-term memory for spoken numbers and letters was very poor, but his short-term memory for visual information was better, and his long-term memory still worked. If STM were a single store, damage to it should affect all kinds of information in the same way. This also raises a problem: if information must pass through STM to reach LTM, how could KF still learn new things? Rehearsal is not the only route into LTM. We remember many things we never repeated to ourselves, such as what happened on our first day at a new school.

items.x: The hippocampus and memory consolidation The hippocampus is a curved structure deep inside each temporal lobe (its name comes from the Greek word for seahorse). We have two, one in each hemisphere. It sits in the medial temporal lobe , close to the amygdala and the entorhinal cortex. A new memory is fragile. A new classmate's name can be lost within seconds. Memory consolidation is the process by which a new, fragile memory becomes stable enough to be stored in long-term memory. When two neurons are repeatedly active together, the synapse between them can become stronger, so a signal passes more easily next time. This is long-term potentiation (LTP) , one of the main proposed mechanisms of learning. items.x: Memory is a reconstruction, not a recording It is tempting to think of memory as a video camera: something happens, it is recorded, and later we press play. Research suggests that this is not how memory works. When we recall an event, we rebuild it from the pieces we stored, and we fill the gaps with what we expect to have happened. This is called reconstructive memory . What guides the rebuilding? A large part of the answer is schemas . A schema is a mental framework of knowledge and expectations about a person, an object, an event or a situation, built up from past experience. items.x: The risk of cultural bias in memory tests A memory test is never culture-free. It uses material, a language and a scoring system, and each of these can favour one group. Material. Bartlett's story was unfamiliar to his English participants, which was the point of the study. A test that uses objects, names or story structures from one culture will make people from another culture look worse at remembering, when they are really less familiar with the content. Scoring. If a test gives more credit to long, detailed, emotional memories, it may reward one culture's way of telling a memory. A brief memory about a family routine is not a weaker memory. It may be a different kind of memory.

items.x: What counts as an environmental factor? Memory has three stages: encoding (getting information in), storage (keeping it) and retrieval (getting it back out). External factors are in the surroundings: the room, sounds, smells and lighting. Internal factors are the state of the person, such as mood or tiredness. items.x: The encoding specificity principle Tulving and Thomson (1973) proposed the encoding specificity principle . items.x: Cognitive load theory Cognitive load theory Cognitive load theory was developed by John Sweller in the late 1980s. It starts from two features of human memory. Working memory , where we consciously think about new information, can only handle a few new elements at once. Long-term memory has no known limit and stores knowledge as schemas , organised units of knowledge that can be handled as one chunk. Learning means building schemas in long-term memory. Because new information has to pass through limited working memory first, teaching works best when it does not overload working memory. The theory describes three types of cognitive load. items.x: What makes a study an experiment? An experiment is the only research method that can test cause and effect directly. The researcher changes one variable, keeps everything else the same, and measures what happens to a second variable. The independent variable (IV) is the variable the researcher changes or compares. The dependent variable (DV) is the variable the researcher measures. It is expected to depend on the IV. Extraneous variables are any other variables that might affect the DV. When an extraneous variable changes along with the IV, it becomes a confounding variable , and the researcher can no longer tell which one caused the change in the DV. Back to the warm-up. items.k: Operationalising variables | operationalised
items.x: Operationalising variables A variable is operationalised when you say exactly how it will be changed or measured. "Memory" is not operationalised. "The number of words correctly recalled from a list of 20, written down within two minutes" is. Operationalising matters because it lets another researcher repeat your study in exactly the same way, and it makes clear what your results can and cannot tell you.

items.k: Hypotheses | research hypothesis | directional | non-directional | null hypothesis
items.x: Hypotheses A research hypothesis predicts the effect of the IV on the DV. It must include both operationalised variables. A directional (one-tailed) hypothesis predicts which way the difference will go, for example "Group A will recall more words than Group B". A non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis predicts only that there will be a difference. The null hypothesis states that the IV will have no effect on the DV, and that any difference found is due to chance.

Usually the IV is a characteristic participants already have, such as age, gender or whether they are bilingual, so participants cannot be randomly allocated to it. A study comparing the recall of Grade 9 and Grade 12 students is a quasi-experiment, because nobody can be randomly allocated to an age. This matters for causality . A bias is a systematic error: something that pushes thinking or findings away from the truth in one particular direction. Compare two faulty kitchen scales. Many things psychologists study, such as intelligence, stress, memory or loneliness, are constructs : ideas that cannot be seen directly. To study them, researchers must operationalise them, which means stating exactly how they will be measured. "Memory" is a construct; "the number of words recalled from a list of 20 after a 30-second delay" is an operationalised variable. Every choice of operationalisation includes some parts of the construct and leaves others out. items.x: Responsibility The question it asks: what do psychologists owe to the people they study and to society? Psychologists study people, and their findings shape treatments, school policies and public opinion. That gives them power, and responsibility is about using it well: during research, when reporting results, and when results are applied. During research , ethical guidelines protect participants: informed consent; the right to withdraw, including withdrawing their data; anonymity and confidentiality; protection from harm; avoiding deception unless it is essential and harmless; and a full debrief afterwards. items.x: Perspective is not bias, and concepts connect This is one of the most common mistakes in exam answers, so it gets its own section. A perspective is a coherent framework that can be partly right: a biological and a sociocultural explanation of anxiety can both be valid. A bias is a distortion that pushes findings away from the truth. Calling a perspective "biased" because it only looks at one kind of cause confuses the two. The accurate point is usually that relying on one perspective alone can lead to a reductionist explanation, which you can then argue as a limitation. A dictionary definition of causality ("one thing causing another") is accurate but does no work. items.s: What makes a study an experiment?

items.x: What makes a study an experiment? Experiments An experiment is a research method in which the researcher deliberately changes one variable, keeps other variables as constant as possible, and measures the effect on a second variable. That combination of manipulation and control is what makes experiments the method best suited to testing cause and effect. The independent variable (IV) is the variable the researcher changes. It is the presumed cause. Each version of it is called a condition . The dependent variable (DV) is the variable the researcher measures. It is the presumed effect. Controlled variables are kept the same in every condition, such as the room, the instructions, the materials

items.k: Operationalising variables and writing hypotheses | operationalised | research hypothesis | directional | non-directional | null hypothesis
items.x: Operationalising variables and writing hypotheses A variable is operationalised when you say exactly how it will be changed or measured. "Memory" is a construct; "the number of words correctly recalled from a list of 20 in 60 seconds" is an operationalised DV. "Music" is vague; "a recording of instrumental music played at the same volume throughout the task" is an operationalised IV. Operationalising matters for two reasons: another researcher can repeat (replicate) the study exactly, and readers can see what the results do and do not tell them. Any operationalisation leaves part of the construct out, which is always worth an evaluation point. A research hypothesis is a testable prediction

items.s: Random allocation is not random sampling
items.k: Random allocation is not random sampling | Random sampling | generalised | Random allocation | cause and effect
items.x: Random allocation is not random sampling These two terms sound alike and are confused in exams more than any other pair. Random sampling is about who takes part : every member of the target population has an equal chance of being chosen. It affects how far the results can be generalised . It is rare in practice. Random allocation is about which condition each participant is placed in, for example by drawing names from a container or using a random number generator. It spreads participant variables across conditions by chance, so no group is systematically different at the start. It affects whether the study can claim cause and effect . items.k: What threatens a causal claim | extraneous variable | confounding variable | Demand characteristics | Researcher effects | controls | Standardisation | Random allocation | Single-blind | double-blind | placebo | pilot study | manipulated | controlled | comes before
items.x: What threatens a causal claim? An extraneous variable is anything other than the IV that could affect the DV: noise, time of day, how tired participants are, how the instructions are read. If an extraneous variable changes along with the IV, it becomes a confounding variable , and the researcher can no longer tell which of the two caused the change in the DV. If the music group did the task in the morning and the silence group after lunch, time of day is a confound. Two further threats come from the people in the study. Demand characteristics: cues that tell participants what the study is about, so that they change their behaviour, often to help (or sometimes to spoil) the result.

items.k: When a true experiment is not possible | true experiment | randomly allocated | It is impossible | It is unethical | It is impractical
items.x: When a true experiment is not possible A true experiment has two features: the researcher manipulates the IV, and participants are randomly allocated to conditions. Together these let the researcher claim that the IV caused any difference in the DV. But random allocation is not always possible, and it is not always ethical. It is impossible when the IV is something participants already have: age, gender, first language, whether they are bilingual, which school they attend. Nobody can be randomly allocated to being 15 or being a Grade 12 student. It is unethical when the IV would harm people: you cannot randomly allocate children to grow up in poverty, or teenagers to lose sleep for a term,

items.x: Quasi-experiments and natural experiments Experiments A quasi-experiment looks like an experiment, with conditions and a measured DV, but participants are not randomly allocated to the conditions. Often the groups already exist: Grade 9 versus Grade 12 students, bilingual versus monolingual students, students who chose to revise with music versus those who chose silence. The researcher may still control the setting and the task, but cannot control who is in which group. A natural experiment is a kind of quasi-experiment in which the IV changes in the real world without the researcher's involvement. items.x: Ethics in psychological research Ethics Ethics is not a checklist; it is a judgement. Researchers weigh the likely benefits of the knowledge against the likely costs to participants. This is a cost-benefit analysis . A small, temporary discomfort may be justified if the study could help many people; serious or lasting harm is not justified by any benefit. The main guidelines are: Guideline What it means Informed consent Participants are told enough about the study, before it starts, to decide freely whether to take part. items.k: What is an observation | observation
items.x: What is an observation? Observations In an observation , the researcher watches and records behaviour as it happens, rather than asking people about it or changing anything. Observations are the method of choice when what people do matters more than what they say they do, and when participants cannot easily report on their own behaviour, as with young children. Observations record what happens, not why. Because the researcher does not manipulate a variable, an observation on its own cannot establish cause and effect. It can describe behaviour in detail, show which behaviours go together, and generate ideas that experiments can then test. Observation is also used inside other methods: an

items.k: Three dimensions of observation design | Naturalistic | Controlled | Overt | Covert | Non-participant | Participant
items.x: Three dimensions of observation design Observations Every observation is described on three separate dimensions, so a single study combines one choice from each. A study can be naturalistic, covert and non-participant, for example. Dimension Option 1 Option 2 Setting Naturalistic: behaviour is watched where it normally happens, without interference. Higher ecological validity, but the behaviour of interest may be rare and many variables are uncontrolled. Controlled: behaviour is watched in a setting the researcher has arranged, such as a playroom with set toys. Easier to standardise and repeat, but behaviour may be less natural. Awareness Overt: participants know they are being watched.

items.x: Deciding what to record: behavioural categories An observer cannot record everything, so the behaviour of interest is broken into behavioural categories , also called a coding scheme or checklist. Good categories are: Operationalised: defined precisely enough that two observers would classify the same behaviour the same way. "Off task" is vague; "eyes away from the work materials for 3 seconds or more" is operationalised. Mutually exclusive: a behaviour fits only one category at a time. items.x: Sampling: who, and when An observation involves two separate sampling decisions, and it is worth keeping them apart. Choosing participants uses the same techniques as any method: opportunity, self-selected, random, stratified or snowball sampling (CRM-07). Sampling behaviour decides when to record: Time sampling: at fixed intervals, for example every 30 seconds, the observer records the category the behaviour fits at that moment. This gives a structured record that is easy to compare between observers, but brief behaviours between intervals are missed. items.k: Making observations reliable: inter-rater reliability | Inter-rater reliability | pilot | Observer bias | reflexivity
items.x: Making observations reliable: inter-rater reliability Inter-rater reliability is the extent to which two or more observers, watching the same behaviour independently, record the same thing. If they agree, the data do not depend on who happened to be observing. A simple way to calculate it with time sampling: Inter-rater reliability (%) = number of intervals where the observers agree ÷ total number of intervals × 100 For example, two observers who agree on 8 of 10 intervals have 80% agreement. items.x: The ethics of observation Overt observation allows informed consent before the study. For children, parents or guardians consent. Covert observation means there is no consent at the time. The general rule is that it is acceptable only in public places where people would expect to be seen by strangers, such as a shopping centre or a park, and never in private places. For class practicals, the IB applies this rule strictly. Recording: in our setting, observers take written notes or tallies only. items.x: Distributions and outliers A distribution is the shape the scores make when plotted. In a normal distribution , scores cluster in the middle and tail off evenly on both sides, in a bell shape. The mean, median and mode are roughly the same. In a positively skewed distribution, most scores are low and a long tail stretches to the right. This often happens when a task is too hard (a floor effect). The mean is usually pulled above the median. In a negatively skewed distribution, most scores are high and the tail stretches to the left, often because a task is too easy (a ceiling effect). items.x: Inferential statistics and significance Inferential statistics Inferential statistics test whether a difference or relationship found in a sample is likely to reflect a real pattern, or could easily have arisen by chance. In psychology, results with p < .05 are usually called statistically significant : if there were really no effect, results this strong would turn up less than 5% of the time. items.x: How the brain is built: maturation Brain maturation is the genetically guided growth and organisation of the brain over time. It follows a broadly similar timetable in every healthy child, in every culture. Maturation does not just mean the brain gets bigger: it becomes more organised and faster at sending signals. The basic unit is the neuron . Each neuron has dendrites , which receive signals, a cell body , and an axon , which carries signals to other neurons. The gap between two neurons is a synapse , where chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) pass the signal on. Many axons are wrapped in myelin , a fatty layer that makes signals travel faster. items.x: Critical periods and sensitive periods Maturation sets the timetable, but the brain also needs the right experience at the right time. A critical period is a window of time in development when a particular experience is needed for a skill or function to develop normally. If the experience is missing during that window, the function may never develop normally, even if the experience comes later. items.x: Two pictures of development: a staircase or a ramp? When a child gets better at thinking, what kind of change is happening? There are two broad answers. A stage theory says development happens in a series of distinct steps, like a staircase. Each stage is a different kind of thinking, not just more of the same. This is called qualitative change . items.x: How effective are stage theories and continuous models? The learning objective asks how effective these theories are. A theory is effective if it describes development accurately, explains why change happens, makes predictions we can test, and is useful in real life, for example in schools. Use these four tests when you evaluate. Strengths of stage theories. Piaget's theory describes a clear, testable sequence, and when his tasks, such as conservation, are repeated in many countries, children usually pass them in a similar order, even if the ages vary. It changed how teachers see children, as active learners rather than empty containers, and supports hands-on learning in the early years.

items.x: Development happens in a social world Some theories describe the child as a "little scientist" who works out the world mostly alone, by exploring and testing. items.x: The zone of proximal development The zone of proximal development (ZPD) is the gap between what a child can do alone and what the child can do with help from an adult or a more capable peer (Vygotsky, 1978). "Proximal" means "next" or "nearest". The ZPD is the set of skills a child is close to mastering. A task the child can already do alone is below the ZPD. Repeating it adds little. A task the child cannot do even with help is above the ZPD. Help does not make it learnable yet. A task the child can do with help is inside the ZPD. items.x: Scaffolding Vygotsky did not use the word "scaffolding". The term comes from Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976), who watched an adult tutor help young children build a pyramid from interlocking wooden blocks. Scaffolding is temporary support that lets a learner complete a task they could not complete alone, and which is removed as the learner becomes more able. Like the scaffolding on a building site, it holds things up while the structure is built, and then it comes down. Wood and colleagues described several things a good tutor does. items.x: Guided participation Barbara Rogoff, an American psychologist, extended Vygotsky's ideas in her book Apprenticeship in Thinking (Rogoff, 1990). She argued that much learning does not look like a lesson at all. Children learn by taking part in the real activities of their families and communities, with more experienced people guiding them. She called this guided participation . Like an apprentice working beside a skilled worker, the child is active: watching, joining in, and taking on more responsibility over time. items.x: Language and culture as tools Vygotsky argued that every culture hands its children tools for thinking . Some are physical, such as a ruler, a calendar or a calculator. A child who learns to write can store a thought and come back to it later. For Vygotsky, language was the most important tool. items.x: What is theory of mind? Cognitive models Theory of mind is the ability to understand that people have mental states, such as beliefs, desires, intentions, knowledge and emotions, and that these mental states guide what they do. It also includes understanding that other people's mental states can be different from your own, and different from reality. It is called a "theory" because we never see another person's mind. We only see what they do and say, and from that we build an explanation. items.x: False-belief tasks Why do researchers focus on false beliefs ? If someone's belief is true, a child can predict their behaviour just by thinking about reality, without thinking about the person's mind at all. A false belief separates the two. items.x: How useful is theory of mind for understanding human development? Strengths. Theory of mind explains a wide range of social behaviour with one idea: children learn that minds represent the world, and can represent it wrongly. It makes testable predictions, and the main age pattern is reliable across 178 studies (Wellman et al., 2001) and several cultures (Callaghan et al., 2005). It links development and cognition, since the same ability helps children communicate, keep secrets, learn from others and think about their own beliefs. It also has practical uses, such as encouraging adults to talk with young children about thoughts and feelings. Limitations. Theory of mind is never observed

items.x: The secure base and the internal working model Two ideas from attachment theory are central to this chapter. A secure base is the role an attachment figure plays when a child explores. The child moves away to play and investigate, checks back by looking or returning, and then explores again. If something frightening happens, the child returns to the attachment figure for comfort (a safe haven). Noura in the warm-up was using her mother as a secure base. Mary Ainsworth, who worked with Bowlby, described this pattern. The idea is that confident exploration depends on feeling safe. The internal working model (IWM) is Bowlby's term for the mental model a child builds from repeated experience

items.x: Ainsworth's attachment types Ainsworth developed a way to observe attachment under controlled conditions: the Strange Situation . A one-year-old and their mother spend about 20 minutes in an unfamiliar playroom while observers record the infant's behaviour across eight short episodes. A stranger enters, the mother leaves twice, and she returns twice. The episodes add a little stress, step by step, so that attachment behaviour becomes visible. Researchers pay most attention to reunion behaviour : what the infant does when the mother comes back. items.x: How attachment may shape the developing self Attachment theory makes three predictions about the self. First, a secure child explores more, so they gain more experience of mastering new things, which may support a sense of competence. Second, the IWM gives the child a basic view of their own worth, which may underlie self-esteem. Third, the IWM shapes expectations of others, so it may influence how a child approaches friendships, teachers and later family relationships. These are predictions, and the evidence for them is mostly correlational. items.x: Attachment across cultures Bowlby and Ainsworth argued that attachment is universal : all human infants are born ready to form attachments. Ainsworth's own early observations were made in Uganda, where she watched infants use their mothers as a base for exploration. So the theory has always claimed to apply everywhere. This is where the etic and emic approaches matter. An etic approach studies behaviour using concepts and tools that are assumed to apply across all cultures, often developed in one culture and then used in others. items.x: Does sensitivity cause secure attachment? Correlational evidence. De Wolff and van IJzendoorn (1997) combined 66 studies with more than 4,000 participants. In the studies that used the Strange Situation and observed sensitivity directly, the correlation between sensitivity and attachment security was about r = .24. That is a real but modest link. The authors concluded that sensitivity is an important but not exclusive condition for security: other parts of parenting matter too. A correlation also leaves alternative explanations open. An infant's temperament , for example, could affect both how easy the infant is to care for and how they behave in the Strange Situation. Experimental

items.x: How useful is attachment theory? Strengths. It explains a pattern seen in infants across many cultures: closeness-seeking under stress and exploration from a secure base. It gave researchers a standardised, replicable observation, the Strange Situation, that has been used in many countries. Its central causal claim has experimental support, since improving sensitivity has increased secure attachment in randomised studies. It has changed hospital and nursery practice. Limitations. The link between attachment and the later self relies mostly on correlational and self-report evidence, so it is hard to separate the effect of the early bond from the effect of a home that stays warm or difficult

Causality Links between sensitivity, attachment and the later self are mostly correlational; van den Boom (1994) used random assignment to test whether sensitivity causes security. Bias Early samples were white, middle-class Americans, and most cross-cultural samples are Western; the Strange Situation may be an imposed etic. items.x: What is enculturation? Enculturation Enculturation is the process by which a person learns the values, beliefs, norms and practices of their own culture, usually from birth and through childhood. It is how a baby becomes a member of a particular community: someone who knows how to greet people, what to wear for a wedding, how to behave in a classroom, and what counts as polite or rude. Most of enculturation happens without a lesson plan. The child watches, copies, is praised or gently corrected, and slowly the rules start to feel "normal". By adolescence, many of these rules feel less like rules and more like "who I am". That is why this topic belongs in the study of the development of self

items.x: Social norms: the unwritten rules A social norm is a shared expectation about how people in a group should behave in a particular situation. Norms are usually unwritten and are not laws. They tell us what is expected (stand when an elder enters) and what is not accepted (interrupting a guest). Three features of norms matter for this chapter: They are learned, not inborn. A baby does not know which hand to use when passing a cup. The rule has to be acquired. They vary between cultures and groups. items.x: Agents of enculturation An agent of enculturation is any person, group or institution that passes on the norms of a culture. Four are especially important in childhood and adolescence. Family. The first and, for young children, the strongest agent. Parents, grandparents and older siblings model behaviour every day and react to what the child does. In many Gulf families, grandparents and the wider extended family play a large part in teaching norms of respect and hospitality. School. Schools teach explicit rules (uniform, lining up, raising your hand) and also a "hidden curriculum" of norms, such as how to address a teacher, when to speak and when to stay quiet. items.x: How do norms become part of the self? The learning objective asks about the role of enculturation in the development of self . The self includes our self-concept ("what I am like"), our identity ("which groups I belong to") and the standards we use to judge our own behaviour. Enculturation shapes all three. A useful way to picture this is as a move from outside to inside : External control. A young child follows a norm because an adult is watching, praising or correcting. The rule belongs to other people. Self-regulation. The child starts to follow the norm when no one is watching, and may correct others ("That is not how we do it!"). items.x: How useful is research on enculturation? Strengths. The research combines different perspectives. Fagot (1978) shows the role of the family, a sociocultural factor, and Martin and Halverson (1983) show the role of the child's own thinking, a cognitive factor. Together they explain both how norms are passed on and why they stick. Naturalistic observation gives a realistic picture of family life, and the research has practical uses, such as helping schools make "unwritten rules" visible for new students. Limitations. items.x: Peers and the developing self A peer is someone of about the same age and status as you: a classmate, a teammate, a friend, or someone in the same online group. Peer influence is any change in a person's attitudes, values or behaviour that comes from being around peers. It can be direct, such as a friend telling you to try something, or indirect, such as noticing what everyone else is wearing and changing your own clothes without a word being said. Peer influence matters for the development of self because the self is partly built from other people's reactions. items.x: Peer culture: children build their own social world Peer influence starts early. The sociologist William Corsaro spent about a year as a participant in an American nursery school (Key study 1). He argued that young children do not simply copy adult culture. items.x: Social comparison: "Am I doing this right?" Leon Festinger's (1954) social comparison theory proposes that people judge their own abilities and opinions by comparing themselves with others, especially when there is no objective standard. There is no exam that tells you how good you are at making friends or how stylish you are, so you look at the people around you. Upward comparison means comparing yourself with someone who seems better off ("She got a 7 and I got a 5"). It can motivate, but it can also lower self-esteem. items.x: Conformity: changing behaviour to fit the group Conformity Conformity is changing your behaviour or beliefs to match those of a group, as a result of real or imagined group pressure. Asch (1951) showed that many participants would sometimes give an obviously wrong answer on a simple line-judging task when the rest of the group gave that answer first. Psychologists usually describe two reasons for conformity (Deutsch and Gerard, 1955): Normative social influence: conforming to be liked and accepted, and to avoid rejection. items.x: Social identity in adolescence Social comparison and conformity explain moment-to-moment influence. Social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner, 1979) explains why groups become part of the self. It proposes that part of our self-concept comes from the groups we belong to, and that we are motivated to feel good about those groups. It describes three processes: Social categorisation: we sort people, including ourselves, into groups (the robotics team, the Year 11s, the people who play the same online game). items.x: How useful is research on peer influence? Strengths. Research on peer influence uses several methods that point the same way. Ethnography (Corsaro) shows peer culture in a real setting; experiments with random allocation (Gardner and Steinberg) show that peers can cause a change in behaviour; brain imaging (Chein et al.) suggests a mechanism. Together they are stronger than any one study. The research also has practical uses: schools can use positive peer influence through mentoring and team projects. Limitations. This can happen when a child is raised in a large institution with many changing carers and no one adult who responds to them in particular. items.x: Critical periods, sensitive periods and neuroplasticity Why would early experience matter more than later experience? One answer comes from the brain. Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change its structure and function in response to experience. In early childhood, the brain forms new connections between neurons very quickly, and connections that are used are strengthened while unused ones are pruned. Some of this growth seems to "expect" certain experiences, such as responsive care, language and play. If those experiences are missing, development may take a different path. This links to the idea of a timing window, which comes in a strong and a weak version. Feature Critical period

items.x: Risk, resilience and protective factors A risk factor is anything that makes a poor outcome more likely, such as poverty, serious family conflict, or a caregiver's severe illness. A protective factor is anything that reduces the effect of risk. Resilience is doing well despite serious adversity. Psychologists now see resilience as a process , not a fixed trait that a child either has or lacks. It depends on what the child brings and on the support around them, and it can grow or shrink over time. items.x: Why do children respond differently? The diathesis-stress model Diathesis-stress model Two children can live through the same difficult event, and one struggles while the other copes. The diathesis-stress model offers an explanation. A diathesis is a vulnerability that a person carries, which may be genetic, biological or psychological (for example, a temperament that reacts strongly to change). Stress is the adversity in the environment. The model proposes that a disorder or difficulty develops when the vulnerability and the stress together pass a threshold. Long longitudinal studies such as ERA and Kauai follow the same people for decades, so they can show how development changes rather than taking a single snapshot. items.k: What is an observation
items.x: What is an observation? In an observation, the researcher watches and records behaviour as it happens. The researcher does not change any variable, so an observation is not an experiment. It answers questions like "What do people do?", "How often?" and "For how long?" It cannot tell us why they do it, and it cannot show cause and effect. Back to the warm-up. Most people are not good at remembering how often they did something ordinary, like picking up a phone. They may also give a number that sounds better than the truth. An observation avoids both problems because the researcher records what people do, not what they say they do. This is the main reason psychologists use observation.

items.k: Four choices every observer makes | Naturalistic | Controlled | Non-participant | Participant | Overt | Covert | Structured | Unstructured
items.x: Four choices every observer makes Each observation can be described with four pairs of terms. Use all four when you describe our class practical in the exam. Choice One option The other option Setting Naturalistic: behaviour is observed where it normally happens, such as a home, a park or a cafe. Ecological validity is usually high, but the researcher has little control. Controlled: behaviour is observed in a setting the researcher has set up, such as a playroom with chosen toys. There is more control, but behaviour may be less natural. Role of the observer Non-participant: the observer watches from outside the group and does not join in. This makes it easier to record accurately.

items.k: Behaviour categories and operational definitions | behaviour categories | operational definition
items.x: Behaviour categories and operational definitions A structured observation needs behaviour categories : the list of behaviours the observer will record. Each category needs an operational definition , which says exactly what counts and what does not. "Uses their phone" is too vague. Does glancing at a notification count? Does a phone lying face up on the table count? If two observers answer these questions differently, they will record different data from the same scene. Clear operational definitions make an observation repeatable and allow different observers to agree.

items.k: Sampling behaviour | Event sampling | Time sampling | Continuous recording | target population | opportunity sample
items.x: Sampling behaviour Observers cannot write down everything, so they decide in advance when and what to record. Event sampling: the observer records every time a target behaviour happens, for example a tally mark each time a person starts using a device. This gives a frequency. Time sampling: the observer records what is happening at set intervals, for example every 60 seconds. This is useful when there is too much behaviour to record all of it. Continuous recording: the observer records how long a behaviour lasts, by noting when it starts and when it stops. This gives a duration. Sampling participants is a separate decision. The target population is the group the researcher wants to learn

items.k: Reliability and bias in observation | Inter-observer reliability | percentage agreement | Observer bias | observer effect
items.x: Reliability and bias in observation Inter-observer reliability is the extent to which two observers watching the same behaviour at the same time record the same data. To check it, two observers record the same people independently, then compare their records. A simple way to measure it is percentage agreement : Percentage agreement = number of agreements, divided by the total number of comparisons, multiplied by 100. Example: two observers compare 20 records and agree on 17 of them. 17 divided by 20 is 0.85, multiplied by 100 is 85%. A common rule of thumb is that 80% or more is acceptable. Low agreement usually means the operational definitions are unclear, or that the observers need more

items.k: Ethics in observation | Public places | Privacy | Consent | No interference | Confidentiality
items.x: Ethics in observation Observation raises its own ethical questions, because the people observed often do not know. Public places. Psychologists generally accept covert observation only in public places where people would expect to be seen by strangers, and only of behaviour anyone there could see. Privacy. In the UAE, the law protects personal privacy: it is against the law to photograph or record people without their consent. In student research, observers record anonymous tallies only. No names, no photographs, no audio or video, and no notes that could identify a person. Consent. In private settings, such as a home, observers need permission first. items.k: Analysing observation data | quantitative data | qualitative data | describe | interpret
items.x: Analysing observation data A structured observation gives quantitative data : counts (frequencies) and times (durations). These are analysed with descriptive statistics, such as totals, means and ranges, and shown in a table or a bar chart. An unstructured observation gives qualitative data : field notes, which are analysed by looking for themes. In both cases, keep two steps apart. First describe what the data show. Then interpret what they might mean.

items.k: How useful is observation | Strengths | Limitations
items.x: How useful is observation? Strengths. Observation records what people do, not what they say they do, so it avoids memory errors and social desirability bias. Naturalistic observation has high ecological validity, because the behaviour happens in a real setting. It is often the only practical method for studying young children, who cannot fill in a questionnaire, and for behaviour people do without thinking, such as picking up a phone. Limitations. Observation cannot explain why people behave as they do, and it cannot show cause and effect. Observer bias and the observer effect can both distort the data. items.x: What acculturation is Models of acculturation Acculturation is the process by which people from one culture come into contact with another culture and take on some of its behaviours, norms and values. It usually follows a move from one culture into another, for migration, study or work. What matters is sustained contact with an unfamiliar set of norms, not the distance travelled to get there. Not to be confused with enculturation. You met enculturation in Human Development: learning your own culture as you grow up, through instruction and social learning. items.s: From one line to two dimensions
items.k: From one line to two dimensions | acculturation strategies
items.x: From one line to two dimensions Models of acculturation Before the 1980s, most researchers treated acculturation as a single line. The more of the new culture a person took on, the more of their heritage culture they were assumed to lose. From the 1970s onwards, John Berry developed a model with two separate dimensions (Berry, 1980; summarised in Berry, 1997). First, how receptive is the person to the new culture? Second, how far do they keep links to their culture of origin? Because the two dimensions are independent, a person can be high on both, low on both, or high on one and low on the other. That gives four acculturation strategies . Strategy Receptive to the new culture? Keeps links

items.k: How acculturation is measured
items.x: How acculturation is measured Acculturation cannot be seen. A researcher can only record things that might stand for it: what someone eats, which language they use at home, who they spend weekends with, how they describe themselves. There are two main approaches: questionnaires and proxy measures. Approach What it records What it assumes One-dimensional questionnaire Items on a single line running from one culture to the other (for example "Spanish only" to "English only", with "both equally" in the middle), as in the original Acculturation Rating Scale for Mexican Americans (ARSMA). Acculturation is a single line. A high score for one culture means a low score for the other.

items.x: What compliance is Compliance techniques Compliance is a change in behaviour in response to a request. The request is what makes it compliance. When you conform, you change your behaviour because the people around you behave a certain way, but no one has asked you to. When you comply, someone has asked. The request can be explicit, like a call for donations, or implicit, like an advertisement. You may not even know you are the target. A compliance technique is a specific strategy for getting the response someone wants. Foot-in-the-door and low-ball are the two you will study here, but there are many others. items.x: What conformity is Conformity Conformity is changing your beliefs, attitudes or behaviour to match those of a group. What sets it apart from other kinds of social influence is that no one asks. There is no request, and often no intention to influence you at all. You adjust because you see what the group does. Psychologists distinguish two reasons for conforming. Informational influence: you are unsure, so you assume the group knows better. The more uncertain you are, the stronger the pull. Yusuf in the canteen is an example. Normative influence: you want to be accepted, so you go along with the group even when you privately disagree. Yusuf's emoji is an example. Not every group pulls

items.k: Variations on the paradigm | One ally changes everything | Group size matters, up to a point | Privacy reduces conformity
items.x: Variations on the paradigm Asch and others changed one feature of the procedure at a time to see what affected conformity. One ally changes everything. When one other person in the group gave the correct answer, conformity dropped sharply. Participants felt warmth towards this person, but often did not recognise that the ally had changed their own behaviour. Group size matters, up to a point. Conformity rose as the majority grew, then levelled off: adding more people made little further difference. Privacy reduces conformity. When participants wrote their answers down instead of saying them aloud, conformity fell. This suggests that much of the conformity in the original study was normative.

Participants No new participants. A meta-analysis of 133 studies that used Asch's line task, run in 17 countries. Procedure The researchers combined the results of the studies and tested which features were linked to higher or lower conformity, including the culture in which each study was run and the year it was carried out. Findings Conformity tended to be higher in collectivist countries than in individualist ones. In the USA, where the paradigm began, conformity had declined since the 1950s.

items.k: A biological basis
items.x: A biological basis? If conformity is so common, it may once have helped our ancestors survive. Pike and Laland (2010) studied nine-spined sticklebacks, a small freshwater fish. The fish first learned from their own experience which of two feeders gave more food. Then they watched other fish feeding in a way that suggested the opposite. When they were free to choose, many followed the other fish instead of their own experience, and they were disproportionately likely to copy what the majority did. Copying the majority may be an old and useful strategy, and not only a human one. Remember that this is animal research: a fish choosing a feeder is a long way from a student sending an emoji.

items.x: Why compare cultures at all? There are two ways to study a culture. In the emic approach , the researcher immerses themselves in one culture and tries to understand it on its own terms, without importing ideas from outside. That is the etic approach , and cultural dimensions are exactly such a set. items.x: Why do groups come into conflict? Before social identity theory, two explanations of conflict between groups were common. Aggressive personality explanations said that conflict happens because some people are aggressive or hostile by nature. They looked inside the person and paid little attention to the social situation. Realistic group conflict theory , developed from the work of Muzafer Sherif in the 1950s, said that conflict is caused by real competition between groups for limited resources, such as land, food, money or a prize.
