items.x: What social identity theory says Social identity theory Social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner, 1979) proposes that part of how we see ourselves, our social identity , comes from the groups we belong to. The theory can be summed up in six claims. Claim In plain words 1 Competition over resources is not always needed for conflict between groups to develop. 2 Simply seeing yourself as a member of one of two groups, called social categorisation , is enough to trigger in-group favouritism and out-group discrimination . 3 Categorising gives people a way to build a social identity. They define themselves as similar to or different from other groups, and as "better" or "worse" than them. 4

items.x: The minimal group paradigm The evidence behind these claims came first. Years before social identity theory was published, Tajfel's team asked what the smallest possible condition for group favouritism was, so they needed groups that were real in the participants' minds and in no other way. The theory was later built partly to explain what they found. They used the minimal group paradigm . Participants are divided into two groups on a trivial basis, such as how they estimated dots on a screen, which painting they preferred, or even a coin toss. items.s: How useful is social identity theory?

items.x: How useful is social identity theory? Strengths. The theory has wide explanatory power. It explains why favouritism and discrimination can appear even when nothing is being competed for. It helps explain how members of lower-status groups respond to their position, for example by trying to leave the group or by finding new ways to see it positively (claim 6). It helps explain stereotyping: if distinctiveness matters for self-esteem, stereotypes that make other groups look worse may matter too. It has led to practical strategies for reducing conflict between groups (see the next section). The experiments behind it were tightly controlled and have been replicated many times. Limitations.

items.x: Social exchange theory Social exchange theory (SET) was proposed by Thibaut and Kelley (1959). It suggests that people make a rational calculation of costs and benefits to decide whether a relationship is worth continuing. It treats a relationship a little like a business: a series of exchanges in which each person hopes to gain as much as possible at the lowest cost. Rewards are what the relationship gives you, such as companionship, support, fun or status. Costs are what the relationship takes from you, such as time, effort, stress or giving up other options. Profit is the rewards minus the costs. A relationship is worth continuing when the profit is high enough. Thibaut and Kelley also

items.x: Equity theory Equity theory , applied to close relationships by Hatfield and Traupmann (1980), suggests that a relationship is stable when both people see it as fair: what each one gets out of it is roughly in proportion to what each one puts in. High profit is not enough. It also has to feel fair. If you feel the other person benefits more than you do, you are likely to feel dissatisfied, even resentful. If you feel you benefit more than the other person does, the relationship is not stable either, because you may feel guilty or uncomfortable. items.x: The investment model of commitment Cognitive models The investment model was proposed by Caryl Rusbult (1980) to explain why people stay in relationships or leave them. It is the main example of a cognitive model in this area. It says that commitment , the intention to continue a relationship, depends on three components. Satisfaction: generally positive feelings about the other person and the relationship. Satisfaction is high when rewards are high and costs are low. Perceived quality of alternatives: what else is on offer. An alternative could be another relationship, but also being alone, or spending the time with family or other friends. items.x: Limitations of the research Rusbult's studies show three problems that are common in this whole area of research. Self-report. It is hard to find anything more objective than asking people about their satisfaction and commitment. It is also hard for participants to tell abstract constructs apart. Will every participant understand the difference between "costs" and "investments" in the same way? Correlational data. Interpretations can be speculative. In Rusbult (1983), for men and for stayers, the greater the costs, the stronger the commitment. That does not fit the model. items.k: How useful are cognitive explanations | Strengths | Limitations | Real life: why do people stay
items.x: How useful are cognitive explanations? Strengths. The models explain something biology finds hard to explain: why people stay in relationships that no longer make them happy, and why commitment changes slowly over months. The investment model makes clear, testable predictions and has been supported by an experiment and by a longitudinal study. The same reasoning applies to friendships, teams and clubs, so the models are useful lenses well beyond romantic relationships. Limitations. The evidence depends heavily on self-report, and the experiments use hypothetical stories. The models assume that people calculate rationally, while much of what happens in relationships is emotional and fast.

items.x: Why study communication? Human beings are social and depend on each other, and communication is how we run a relationship from day to day. It is how we make contact, resolve conflict and move from being strangers to being close. Positive relationships are a major source of well-being and help protect people against health problems, so how people communicate matters well beyond any single conversation. Research on relationships was not always taken seriously. items.x: Conflict and six styles of resolving it Conflict is a normal part of relationships, and it is not necessarily bad. Depending on how it is handled, people can come out of it with a stronger relationship than before. Learning to resolve conflict constructively may be more valuable than simply avoiding it. Guerrero, Andersen and Afifi (2021) described six styles of conflict resolution, placed along two dimensions: uncooperative to cooperative (is each person trying to win, or trying to find a solution that works for both?) and direct to indirect (do they talk about the issue openly, or avoid it?). items.x: The Sound Relationship House John and Julie Gottman described the theory behind their therapy as the Sound Relationship House . In this model, two "weight-bearing walls", trust and commitment , hold a relationship together at all times. Trust lets people rely on each other. Commitment gives a sense of certainty that their intentions are serious and that problems are temporary. On top of the walls sit seven "floors": the things two people can work on to improve their relationship. Each floor rests on the one below it, and a couple who reach the top floor have a good chance of a lasting, sound relationship. The Gottmans describe the house for couples. items.k: What the therapy involves | assessment | plan | sessions | education
items.x: What the therapy involves Gottman-method couples therapy usually begins with an assessment : a joint session, individual interviews with each partner, and questionnaires. The therapist then designs a plan for the couple, followed by a series of sessions with specific assignments and tasks to practise at home. The therapy also includes education : the therapist teaches the clients evidence-based principles of healthy relationships. At its core is making the clients more aware of the important parts of their relationship, and of the positive and negative patterns in how they communicate.

items.x: What is a survey? A survey collects self-report data: people answer questions about their own attitudes, opinions, experiences or behaviour. Strictly, the survey is the whole process of collecting the answers, and the questionnaire is the list of questions. The IB uses the two words interchangeably, so you can use either in the exam. Surveys are the method of choice when you want to know what many people think, quickly and cheaply. You have already met a very large one: Hofstede's values questionnaire, answered by more than 100,000 IBM employees ( HR-04 ). Two limits are worth learning now. A survey records what people say , not what they do . And a survey changes nothing: it measures

items.k: Likert scales and ordinal data | Likert scale | ordinal | median | mode
items.x: Likert scales and ordinal data A Likert scale asks people to rate agreement or importance on a fixed scale, for example from 1 (not at all important) to 5 (extremely important). Labelling every point, not just the ends, helps everyone read the scale the same way. The numbers on a Likert scale have an order, so the data are ordinal . But nothing guarantees that the gap between 4 and 5 means the same as the gap between 1 and 2, and one person's 4 may be another person's 5. That is why Likert data are usually summarised with the median (the middle rating) and the mode (the most common rating), or with the percentage of people who chose the top points. items.x: Writing good items One idea per item. "Funny and supportive" is two qualities, so an answer cannot tell you which one the person was rating (a double-barrelled item). No hint about the answer you want. "Don't you agree..." pushes people towards yes (a leading item). Plain, specific words. A term like "emotional intelligence" means different things to different people. Describe the behaviour instead, so the item is operationalised. Clear, complete choices. "Often" and "sometimes" are read differently by different people; give choices with clear meanings, and make sure every answer has somewhere to go. Sensitive or personal items last, and optional. items.k: Cross-sectional and longitudinal surveys | cross-sectional | longitudinal
items.x: Cross-sectional and longitudinal surveys A cross-sectional survey compares different groups at one point in time, like a snapshot: for example, Grade 11 and Grade 12 students answering in the same week. It is quick, but the groups differ in more ways than their grade, so a difference between them cannot be read as change. A longitudinal survey asks the same people the same questions more than once, for example in Grade 11 and again in Grade 12. It can show change within people, but it takes much longer, and some participants drop out along the way.

items.k: Ethics in surveys | Explicit informed consent | Age | Anonymity | The right to withdraw | No distressing questions
items.x: Ethics in surveys The guide notes that surveys raise fewer ethical issues than many methods, but consent must still be given before anyone answers. Explicit informed consent: participants read what the survey is about and tick to agree. Simply filling it in does not count as consent. Age: participants under 16 need written consent from a parent or guardian. Anonymity: no names, and no details that together could identify someone in a small sample. The right to withdraw: stop at any time, skip optional items, and have answers removed afterwards. With anonymous data, a made-up code is one way to make this possible. No distressing questions , and data stored privately, used only for the study

At break, lunch or after school, we asked a Grade 11 or Grade 12 student, using the same short script, whether they would take part. If they agreed, we entered our researcher number, handed over the device, and stepped away while they read the information and answered. The disorder we will use throughout this unit is major depressive disorder (MDD) , so you can look at one condition through biological (this chapter), cognitive and sociocultural lenses, and then at its treatment. items.x: What a biological explanation tries to do A biological explanation looks for the cause of a disorder in the body. For MDD, researchers have looked at three levels: chemical messengers in the brain (neurotransmission), the genes a person inherits (genetic inheritance), and the structure of the brain. Each level is studied with different tools, and each has its own problems of measurement and causality.

items.x: Neurotransmission and the serotonin hypothesis Neurotransmission Neurotransmission is how neurons communicate. When a signal reaches the end of the presynaptic neuron, it releases a neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft , the tiny gap between neurons. The neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron and changes how likely that neuron is to fire. Afterwards, the neurotransmitter is taken back into the presynaptic neuron by a transporter protein. This is called reuptake . items.x: The serotonin hypothesis today In 2022, Moncrieff et al. published an umbrella review : a review of existing systematic reviews, meta-analyses and large studies. They included 17 studies across six areas of evidence, such as serotonin levels in body fluids, serotonin receptors, the serotonin transporter, experiments that temporarily lower tryptophan (the building block the body uses to make serotonin), and genetic studies of the serotonin transporter gene. They found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by lower serotonin activity or concentration, and concluded that the serotonin theory of depression is "not empirically substantiated". Two points matter when you use this study.

items.x: Genetic inheritance: what twin studies show Genetic inheritance Genetic inheritance is the passing of genes from parents to children. If MDD has a genetic component, close relatives of people with MDD should be more likely to develop it. But families share homes, habits and stressors as well as genes, so a family pattern on its own cannot separate genes from environment. Twin studies try to solve this. Monozygotic (MZ, identical) twins share almost all of their genes. Dizygotic (DZ, non-identical) twins share about half, like ordinary siblings. items.x: The diathesis-stress model Diathesis-stress model The diathesis-stress model says that a disorder develops when a diathesis (a pre-existing vulnerability) meets enough stress (difficult experiences in the environment). A diathesis can be biological, such as genetic risk, or psychological, such as a habit of negative thinking. Stress can be a single event, such as losing a job, or a build-up of smaller pressures over time. So a person with a strong vulnerability may not develop depression if their life is relatively free of major stress, and a person with little vulnerability may cope with a stressful year. items.x: Biological reductionism Biological reductionism Biological reductionism is the attempt to explain complex behaviour by reducing it to its simplest biological parts, such as one neurotransmitter or one gene. In the warm-up, the same unanswered message could mean "everyone is busy" or "nobody likes my ideas". A cognitive model asks why some people reliably reach for the second reading. items.x: Negative schemas and early experience Schema theory Why would someone develop these views? Beck's answer uses schema theory . A schema is a mental framework of knowledge and beliefs, built from experience, that guides how we process new information. We have schemas for places, people, events and ourselves. Schemas let us process information quickly, but they also make us see what we expect to see. Beck proposed that some people develop negative self-schemas through early experiences, for example repeated criticism, the loss of a parent, or being rejected or bullied. items.x: Automatic negative thoughts and cognitive distortions Once a schema is active, it produces automatic negative thoughts (often shortened to ANTs). These are fast, involuntary thoughts that appear in response to a situation. The person usually does not notice them as thoughts; they simply feel true. An essay handed back with comments might trigger "I am stupid" before the comments are even read. Beck argued that these thoughts come from systematic errors in reasoning, which he called cognitive distortions . Everyone makes these errors sometimes. items.x: How negative beliefs keep themselves going: confirmation bias Confirmation bias If negative beliefs are false, why does new experience not correct them? The answer lies in confirmation bias : the tendency to search for, notice, interpret and remember information that fits what we already believe, and to overlook information that does not. A negative self-schema works like a filter at each stage of processing: Attention: the person notices the frown in the audience but not the people nodding. Interpretation: ambiguous events, like an unanswered message, are read in the most negative way. Memory: failures are recalled more easily than successes, so the past seems to confirm the belief.

items.x: Cause or symptom? This is the central debate about cognitive models. Depressed people clearly think more negatively than non-depressed people. But that fact alone cannot tell us which came first. There are three possibilities: Cause: negative schemas and thinking come first and make depression more likely. This is Beck's claim. Symptom: depression comes first, and negative thinking is part of what being depressed is like. When the depression lifts, the thinking improves. Both: negative thinking raises the risk of depression, and depression in turn makes thinking more negative, which keeps the cycle going. items.x: How useful are cognitive models of depression? Strengths. Cognitive models explain the content of depressive thinking, which biological explanations do not: why a person feels worthless, not just why they feel low. items.x: How useful is cross-cultural research on depression? Strengths. Large etic surveys use the same interview in many countries, so differences cannot be blamed on different questions. Emic research, like Kleinman's, shows how culture shapes the way depression is felt and described, and it has changed practice: the DSM-5 now includes the Cultural Formulation Interview. Research on adapted treatments, such as the Friendship Bench, shows how to reach people who would never visit a psychiatrist. Limitations. It is very hard to separate true prevalence from recorded prevalence, because the same cultural factors (stigma, somatisation, help-seeking) affect both the illness and the measurement.

items.x: What counts as an environmental factor? An environmental factor is anything outside the person that may raise or lower their risk of a mental health disorder: what happens to us (life events), the conditions we live in (chronic stress), the people around us (social support and networks), what we learn from others (social learning), the groups we belong to (social identity), and what happened to us as children (childhood adversity). Environmental factors rarely act alone. items.k: How useful are environmental explanations of depression | Strengths | Limitations
items.x: How useful are environmental explanations of depression? Strengths. Environmental research explains what biology alone cannot: why depression often begins after a loss, and why it is more common in some communities. The links with severe events and lack of a confidant appeared again in Costello's replication. Longitudinal studies measure the environment before later depression, which helps with direction. The research is also useful: if support and group membership protect, schools and communities can build them. Limitations. Most evidence is correlational, so genes, poverty or shared neighbourhoods may explain the links. The arrow can point both ways: depressed people lose friends.

items.x: How useful is social learning theory for understanding social media addiction? Strengths. It explains how social media habits spread through families and friend groups without anyone deliberately teaching them. It fits the evidence: Sherman et al. showed experimentally that visible peer approval changes teenagers' behaviour, and Hefner et al. found that parents' own phone habits go with their children's. It explains why some models matter more than others, through identification and status. It also has practical uses: if the problem is partly learned from models, prevention can use models too, such as parents keeping to their own rules or older students modelling healthy use. items.x: Stressors and the stress response A stressor is an event or situation that places demands on a person, such as an exam, an argument or an illness in the family. Stress is the state a person is in when those demands feel too much for them. Stress can be acute (short-term, such as the hour before a presentation) or chronic (long-term, such as months of worry about money or a family member's health). When the brain detects a threat, the body responds through two systems. Both start in the hypothalamus , and both use chemical messengers . items.x: Stress as a transaction: Lazarus and Folkman (1984) Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman proposed the transactional model of stress and coping in their book Stress, Appraisal, and Coping (1984). Their key claim is that stress is not a fixed property of an event. It is a transaction (an exchange) between a person and their situation. A situation becomes stressful when a person judges that its demands are greater than the resources they have to deal with it, and that their well-being is at stake. items.x: Social media as a way of coping Social media is always available, it is free, and it changes how we feel within seconds. That makes it an obvious emotion-focused coping tool. A student who picks up their phone between revision sessions is often not choosing social media for its own sake. They are choosing a break from a feeling. Posting, liking and replying can also bring social support, which can help. Researchers have suggested several reasons why this kind of coping can become harder to control: Relief works as a reward. If scrolling reduces an unpleasant feeling, the behaviour is negatively reinforced (operant conditioning), so it becomes more likely the next time the feeling returns.

items.x: How SSRIs work: reuptake inhibition Neurotransmission Neurons communicate by neurotransmission . Here is what normally happens at a serotonin synapse: An electrical signal (an action potential) travels down the presynaptic neuron to its terminal. The signal causes small sacs called vesicles to release serotonin into the synaptic cleft , the tiny gap between two neurons. Serotonin binds to receptors on the postsynaptic neuron. This makes the next neuron more or less likely to fire. The signal is then switched off. Most serotonin is pulled back into the presynaptic neuron by a protein called the serotonin transporter . items.x: The time-lag puzzle An SSRI starts blocking reuptake within hours of the first tablet. Yet the NHS advises that antidepressants usually take one to two weeks to start having an effect, and the full benefit can take longer. items.x: Side effects, in general terms SSRIs are usually offered before older antidepressants because their side effects are generally easier to manage. Common ones include feeling sick, headaches, changes in sleep and appetite, and feeling restless or anxious, especially in the first weeks. Many ease after a couple of weeks. Doctors see people often when they first start, and monitor young people especially closely. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so stopping is planned with the doctor. For under-18s, the NHS advises that antidepressants are usually not recommended for depression, although they are sometimes used alongside other treatment.

A psychological treatment aims to reduce symptoms by changing how a person thinks, behaves or relates to others, usually through sessions with a trained therapist. items.x: From Beck's model to CBT Aaron Beck's cognitive model proposes that depression is maintained by negative thinking. Remember the three parts: The negative cognitive triad: negative views of the self ("I am a failure"), the world ("nobody cares") and the future ("it will never get better"). Negative schemas: deep beliefs, often formed through earlier experience, that act as filters. When a stressful event activates them, information that fits the schema is noticed and information that does not fit is ignored. Negative automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions: quick thoughts that pop up in a situation and feel true, such as overgeneralisation ("I failed one quiz, so I fail at everything")

items.s: Technique 1: identifying and challenging automatic thoughts
items.k: Technique 1: identifying and challenging automatic thoughts | catch | thought record | test | Socratic questioning | replace | cognitive restructuring | behavioural experiment
items.x: Technique 1: identifying and challenging automatic thoughts The first step is to catch automatic thoughts. A therapist may ask the client to keep a thought record : each time their mood drops, they write down the situation, the thought, the feeling and how strongly they believe the thought. The second step is to test the thought. The therapist does not simply say "that is not true". They ask questions that help the client examine it, a method called Socratic questioning : What is the evidence for and against this thought? Which distortion might this be? What would you say to a friend who thought this? The third step is to replace the thought with a more balanced one that fits the evidence.

items.k: Technique 2: behavioural activation | Behavioural activation | activity scheduling | mastery | pleasure
items.x: Technique 2: behavioural activation Behavioural activation targets withdrawal. People with depression often wait until they feel like doing things, but the motivation does not come. Behavioural activation reverses the order: do the activity first, and mood may follow. The client and therapist plan small, specific activities into the week, a method called activity scheduling . The client rates each activity for mastery (a sense of achievement) and pleasure . A walk with a cousin after Maghrib prayer or helping a parent cook can count. Behavioural activation links back to Beck's model. Each completed activity is evidence against thoughts such as "I cannot do anything" or "nothing is enjoyable

items.x: Relapse: does the effect last? Depression often returns, so relapse prevention is one of the strongest arguments for CBT. In Hollon et al. (2005), people who recovered with cognitive therapy relapsed much less than people switched to placebo, and about as often as people who stayed on medication. One explanation is that CBT teaches skills that the person keeps after therapy ends, while medication helps for as long as it is taken. The picture is not completely clear. Cuijpers et al. (2023) found a small advantage for CBT over medication at 6 to 12 months, but it rested on few trials. Over longer follow-ups, the advantage of CBT over control groups became smaller.

items.x: Treatment strategies CBT-based approaches. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) has been adapted for problematic internet and social media use. Cognitive dissonance Cognitive dissonance Cognitive dissonance is the uncomfortable feeling a person has when they hold two cognitions (beliefs, attitudes or knowledge about their own behaviour) that do not fit together. The theory was proposed by Leon Festinger in 1957. It says that people are motivated to reduce this discomfort, and they can do it in two main ways: change the behaviour, or change the cognitions so that the behaviour seems acceptable. items.x: Where the coding framework comes from Lazarus and Folkman (1984) described stress as a transaction between a person and a situation. The person appraises the situation (is this a threat?) and their own resources (can I cope?). They then distinguished two broad types of coping : Problem-focused coping targets the cause of the stress in practical ways, for example making a plan, managing time or asking for information. Emotion-focused coping tries to reduce the negative feelings that the stress produces, without changing the situation itself, for example distraction, looking at the situation more positively, or seeking comfort. The same behaviour can serve either purpose. Talking to a friend

items.s: Know the task before you start
items.k: Know the task before you start
items.x: Aim Know the task before you start The extended essay is an independent piece of research of up to 4,000 words. In psychology it is a review of published research: you analyse peer-reviewed studies on one focused question, build an argument, weigh the evidence against it, and reach a reasoned judgement. By the end of this stage you can: say what a psychology EE is, and what it is not allowed to be spot topics that will not work before you spend hours on them explain the five criteria in your own words plan your 40 hours and your three reflection sessions Our example question To what extent does taking notes by hand rather than on a laptop improve students' learning from lectures? Based on the IB extended essay guide and the psychology subject-specific guidance (first assessment 2027), paraphrased.

items.x: The task What a psychology EE is It is A review of peer-reviewed research on one focused question About behaviour or cognitive processes, usually through a biological, cognitive or sociocultural lens An argument: a clear line from question to judgement, with counter-arguments weighed Aware of complexity and of what research still cannot tell us It is not Your own experiment, survey, interview or observation (not allowed) A description of a topic, or a summary of a textbook An explanation of how a biological mechanism works, without the behaviour A personal opinion piece 4,000 words at most; examiners stop reading after that About 40 hours of your own time 3 reflection sessions: first, interim and the viva voce 500 words at most for your reflective statement, written after the viva

items.x: How it is marked The five criteria in plain words A 6 Framework B 6 Knowledge and understanding C 6 Analysis and line of argument D 8 Discussion and evaluation E 4 Reflection Criterion In psychology, it asks you to... Where on this site A Framework Ask a focused question about behaviour, choose research that suits it and explain how you chose it, and follow the structure of an academic essay. Find and judge sources, read and take notes, and build your argument. Interim reflection session. Discuss your progress and your argument so far. One full draft. Your supervisor reads and comments on one complete draft. They will not edit it for you, so make it a genuine, complete draft. Final essay. Revise, check and submit the final version. Viva voce. A short final interview with your supervisor about your work and what you learned. The essay is not changed afterwards. Reflective statement. items.s: A good question does half the work
items.k: A good question does half the work
items.x: Aim A good question does half the work Your research question shapes everything that follows: what you search for, which studies you keep, and whether you can build an argument at all. The IB guidance asks for a question clearly focused on behaviour and limited in scope. By the end of this stage you can: narrow a topic you care about into one focused question test a question against five checks and avoid the common traps check that enough research exists before you commit define the key terms in your question Our example question To what extent does taking notes by hand rather than on a laptop improve students' learning from lectures?

items.k: Five checks for any question | One focus | A real debate | Behaviour or thinking | Limited scope | Answerable from published studies | Phrasing
items.x: The checks Five checks for any question One focus. One factor and one outcome, not a list. A real debate. Published research disagrees, or the answer depends on something. If everyone agrees, there is nothing to argue. Behaviour or thinking. The question is about what people (or animals) do, feel or think. Limited scope. It can be answered well in 4,000 words. Answerable from published studies. Enough peer-reviewed research exists, roughly eight or more relevant studies. Phrasing "To what extent..." and "How far..." invite a weighed judgement. "What is..." and "Describe..." invite a description, which cannot earn many marks for argument and evaluation.

items.k: Common traps
items.x: Avoid these Common traps Trap Example Fix Too broad "Social media and mental health" Name one behaviour and one outcome Nature versus nurture "Is aggression genetic or learned?" Choose one specific factor and one measured outcome A population with no research "...in teenagers in Dubai" Only limit the population if studies of that group exist Comparing two treatments "Is therapy A better than therapy B?" Only if trials compare them directly A theory applied to something new "How does schema theory explain a viral trend?" Only if research tests the theory in that situation Pure biology "How does serotonin work?" Focus on the behaviour the biology affects

Then define the terms. In your introduction, say what "learning" means in the studies you use (scores on factual and conceptual questions), and who the "students" were.

items.x: Check yourself Five quick questions Why is "What are the effects of video games?" a weak question? It is too broad (which games, which effects, on whom?) and invites a description rather than an argument. When can you limit your question to a particular population? items.s: Find the research your essay will stand on
items.k: Find the research your essay will stand on
items.x: Aim Find the research your essay will stand on A psychology EE is a review of published, peer-reviewed research. You are not allowed to run your own experiments, interviews or surveys, so the quality of your essay depends on the quality of what you find. By the end of this stage you can: tell which kinds of source can carry your argument and which can only point you to one build a search string and run it in at least two databases use citation chaining to find older and newer studies on the same question keep a search log that becomes the method paragraph in your introduction Our example question on every EE page To what extent does taking notes by hand rather than on a laptop improve students' learning from lectures? Based on the IB's subject-specific guidance for the psychology extended essay (first assessment 2027), paraphrased.

items.k: What counts as a source | Rule of thumb
items.x: Know your sources What counts as a source Not every source does the same job. The IB guidance is clear that reading abstracts alone is not enough: you need to read the studies themselves, especially the method and the discussion. Source Use it to Can it carry your argument? Original peer-reviewed studies Give the evidence: what was done, to whom, and what was found Yes. These are your core sources. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews See the overall pattern across many studies, and how big an effect is Yes, and they help you find the original studies Textbooks and this site Understand an area and its key terms before you search No. Use them to learn, then go to the studies Preprints (for example PsyArXiv) See very recent work Only with care: they are not yet peer reviewed, so say so News stories, blogs, videos Find out that a study exists No. Find and read the original paper Rule of thumb Most of your core evidence should come from the last 15 to 20 years. Older classic studies are fine for context and theory. Eight to fifteen core studies is a sensible range, but this is advice, not an IB rule.

items.k: Databases worth knowing | Paywall
items.x: Where to search Databases worth knowing Where Best for Tip Your school library databases The most reliable psychology coverage (for example APA PsycInfo or JSTOR, if your school subscribes) Ask the librarian which ones you can use and how to log in from home Google Scholar A broad first search Use "Cited by" and "Related articles" under each result PubMed and Europe PMC Health, clinical and brain research Filter for free full text ERIC Learning, memory in school, development and education Tick "Peer reviewed only" Semantic Scholar Free search with citation links Good for finding review articles Unpaywall and DOAJ Finding a legal free copy; checking an open-access journal is genuine Unpaywall is a browser add-on that shows a free copy when one exists Paywall? Ask your librarian, look for the author's own copy on their university page, or email the author politely. Researchers are usually happy to share. Do not use websites that copy paywalled papers illegally.

items.k: Build a search string | AND narrows | OR widens | Quotation marks keep a phrase together | An asterisk catches word endings | Brackets group the synonyms | For our example question | Search for the other side on purpose
items.x: Search like a researcher Build a search string Split your question into its main ideas, list other words for each idea, then join them with a few simple operators. & AND narrows Every result must contain both ideas: laptop AND memory . | OR widens Any of the words will do. Use it for other words that mean the same idea: (recall OR memory OR learning) . “ Quotation marks keep a phrase together "note taking" finds the phrase, not pages that mention notes and taking separately. * An asterisk catches word endings replicat* finds replicate, replication and replicated. Most library databases accept this; Google Scholar ignores it. ( ) Brackets group the synonyms Keep each idea's OR list inside brackets so the database reads it as one idea. For our example question: (laptop OR typing OR typed) AND ("note taking" OR "note-taking" OR notetaking) AND (recall OR "test performance" OR learning) Search for the other side on purpose Run the same search again with AND (replicat* OR meta-analysis OR "no difference") added. Evidence that challenges your argument is as important as evidence that supports it, and it rarely turns up on the first page by itself. Build and run strings quickly with the

items.k: Citation chaining | Backward: older work | Forward: newer work
items.x: Follow the trail Citation chaining One good paper leads to many others. Chaining is often faster and more precise than keyword searching. Backward: older work Read the reference list of a strong paper. It shows you the studies and theories that paper was built on. Forward: newer work In Google Scholar, click "Cited by" under a paper. It shows you later studies that used, tested or challenged it, including failed replications. Forward chaining matters most for famous studies. For our example question, the famous 2014 laptop study has been cited more than a thousand times, and some of those later papers tried to repeat it and could not. You only find that out by looking forward.

items.k: Six steps, then stop | Read one recent review article | Build two or three search strings | Skim titles and abstracts | Chain backward and forward | Stop when the same studies keep appearing
items.x: A routine that works Six steps, then stop Read one recent review article on your topic to get the map of the field and the key terms researchers use. Build two or three search strings from those key terms and run them in at least two databases. Skim titles and abstracts to decide what to open. Log every search as you go. Chain backward and forward from the two or three strongest papers. Save the full text and the DOI straight away. Finding a paper twice wastes an evening. Stop when the same studies keep appearing. That is a good sign you have found the core of the field.

items.k: Your log becomes your method | Weak method paragraph | Strong method paragraph
items.x: Keep a search log Your log becomes your method For a literature review, the "research methods" part of Criterion A is how you searched and selected your studies. A search log gives you that paragraph almost for free. Record the date, where you searched, the exact string, roughly how many results, and how many you kept. Weak method paragraph "I searched online for studies about laptops and memory and chose the most relevant ones." Strong method paragraph "I searched Google Scholar and a library database using three groups of terms (note-taking medium, note-taking, learning outcomes). I included peer-reviewed experiments and meta-analyses that compared handwritten and typed notes and measured test performance, and excluded studies of reading on screens. Forward citation searching from Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) added two replications." The strong version says where, how, what was included and excluded, and why. A reader could repeat it. Keep your log in the search log tool or in your researcher's reflection space.

items.k: Spot a doubtful journal | Warning signs | Good signs
items.x: Be a sceptic Spot a doubtful journal Some "journals" publish almost anything for a fee. No single sign proves a journal is doubtful, but several together should worry you. Warning signs Peer review promised in days, not weeks Invitations to publish sent by unrequested email A scope covering many unrelated fields Editors with no named universities No DOIs, no ISSN, no received and accepted dates Claims of an "impact factor" from an unknown website Good signs Indexed in PubMed, PsycInfo or Scopus Listed in DOAJ if it is open access A named editorial board at real institutions A clear peer-review and ethics policy DOIs on every article Published corrections when mistakes are found Charging authors a fee to publish open access is normal for many good journals. It is only a warning sign when other signs come with it.

items.k: Search sprint
items.x: Exercise 1 · 20 minutes Search sprint Use our example question, or your own if you already have one. Split the question into two to four main ideas. List at least two other words for each idea. Build three search strings: a simple one, a full one with OR groups, and a "challenge" one that looks for replications or meta-analyses. Run them in at least two different databases. Log every search: date, where, the exact string, roughly how many results, how many you kept, and why you changed the string next. Finish with a list of the studies you would read in full. EE-03-1 Keep your log and list in your researcher's reflection space.

items.k: Five quick questions
items.x: Check yourself Five quick questions Why is reading the abstract not enough? An abstract leaves out the details you need to judge and use a study: who took part, how the variables were measured, and the authors' own limitations. The IB guidance says abstracts alone cannot support an EE. What is the difference between AND and OR in a search? AND narrows: results must contain both ideas. OR widens: results can contain any of the words, so you use it for synonyms of one idea. What does forward chaining find that backward chaining cannot? Newer work that cites the paper, including replications, critiques and meta-analyses. Backward chaining only finds older work the paper was built on. Can you use a preprint as a core source? Only with care. A preprint has not been peer reviewed yet. If you use one, say so in your essay and treat its findings as less certain. Why keep a search log? It becomes the method paragraph of your introduction (part of Criterion A), it stops you repeating searches, and it shows your supervisor how you built your literature base.

items.s: Not everything you find belongs in your essay
items.k: Not everything you find belongs in your essay
items.x: Aim Not everything you find belongs in your essay The IB guidance asks you to justify every study you choose by linking it clearly to your research question, and to evaluate each one on its own strengths and limitations rather than with generic points. By the end of this stage you can: score any source with four questions: Match, Method, Merit and Role say what kind of claim a study's design can and cannot support give every study you keep a clear job in your argument write evaluation that is about this study and your question Our example question To what extent does taking notes by hand rather than on a laptop improve students' learning from lectures?

items.k: Match, Method, Merit, Role | Match | Method | Merit | Role | 6 to 8 | 3 to 5 | 0 to 2 | Any | A prompt, not a formula
items.x: The check Match, Method, Merit, Role M Match Does it study the same thing as your question, measured in a way that fits, with people close enough to the ones you are asking about? M Method Can its design support the kind of claim you want to use it for: cause and effect, or only an association? M Merit How much can you trust it? Peer review, sample, replication, how recent it is, and who paid for it. R Role What job will it do in your argument: support, challenge, qualify, or give context? Question 0 1 2 Match A different construct or outcome Related, but a different measure, setting or group The same construct and outcome, a similar group Method The design cannot support your claim Partly: with clear limits you must state The design fits the claim Merit Weak: not peer reviewed, tiny or biased sample, conflict of interest Mixed: some strengths, some real limits Strong: peer reviewed, good sample, replicated or a meta-analysis Role No clear job Background only A clear job in the argument 6 to 8 Keep: a core source 3 to 5 Park: background, or a counter-argument 0 to 2 Cut it Any Borderline? Talk to your supervisor A prompt, not a formula The score starts a conversation; it does not

items.s: Is it really about your question?
items.k: Is it really about your question
items.x: Match Is it really about your question? The most common mistake is keeping a study that is about a nearby idea. Check three things. Check Off-target On-target The construct Screen time, or reading on a tablet The medium used to take notes The outcome Self-reported "memory problems" Scores on a test of the lecture content The people and setting Office workers in meetings Students learning from lectures or lessons A partial match is not a reason to cut, but it is a limitation you must name. Most note-taking studies used university students and short recorded talks, so an essay about school students should say how far those findings can travel.

items.s: What claim can the design support?
items.k: What claim can the design support
items.x: Method What claim can the design support? Design Can support Cannot support Revise True experiment (random allocation) Cause and effect, in that setting That the effect holds outside the lab or over longer periods CRM-03 Quasi- or natural experiment Cause and effect, with caution Ruling out pre-existing differences between groups CRM-04 Correlational study or survey A relationship and its strength Which variable causes which CRM-07 Interviews and other qualitative work How people experience something, and possible reasons why How common it is, or what causes what CRM-06 Case study Depth on one person or group, and new questions Generalising to others CRM-07 Meta-analysis The overall pattern and size of an effect Anything better than the studies it includes Matching the strength of your wording to the design is part of using causality well.

items.s: How much can you trust it?
items.k: How much can you trust it | Peer review | Sample | Replication | Recency | Funding and interests | Openness
items.x: Merit How much can you trust it? Peer review. Has it been checked by other researchers before publication? Sample. How many people, and who? A small sample can produce a large result by chance. There is no magic number: what counts as big enough depends on the design and the size of the effect. How the sample was chosen often matters more than its size. Replication. Has anyone repeated it? What did they find? Famous studies are not always the most reliable ones. Recency. Is it recent enough, or has newer work replaced it? Funding and interests. Who paid for it? Does anyone involved gain from a particular result? Openness. Was it preregistered, and are the data available? A bonus, not a requirement. These are bias and measurement questions, the same ones you use in Papers 1 and 2.

items.k: Give every study a job | Generic evaluation | Specific evaluation | Ethics
items.x: Role Give every study a job Criteria C and D reward a line of argument. A study with a clear job is easy to link back to your question; a study with no job is padding. Job Sentence starter Support "This study supports the claim that ... because ..." Challenge "This study challenges the claim that ... because ..." Qualify "This study suggests the effect depends on ..., because ..." Context "This study shows why ... matters / how ... is defined, which I use to ..." Generic evaluation "This was a lab experiment, so it lacks ecological validity." Specific evaluation "Students watched a short recorded talk and took a quiz soon afterwards without reviewing their notes. My question is about learning across a unit, when students do review, so this study tells us about the first stage only." The specific version names a feature of this study and says what it means for your question. That is what the IB guidance means by avoiding a formulaic approach. Ethics The IB guidance notes that ethics is rarely worth evaluating in an EE unless it limits what the research can tell us. One exception is useful: ethics can explain why some evidence does not exist at all.

items.s: Signs your source list needs work
items.k: Signs your source list needs work
items.x: Red flags Signs your source list needs work An abstract is about a nearby idea, not your exact one. The sample or setting is far from your question and your essay never says so. One study carries the whole argument. Every source agrees with you. You probably have not looked for the other side yet. You are citing a study from a summary you read, not from the paper itself.

items.k: Five quick questions
items.x: Check yourself Five quick questions A survey finds that students who use laptops more get lower grades. Can you use it to argue that laptops cause lower grades? No. A survey shows a relationship, not a cause. Students who use laptops more might differ in other ways, such as how much they study. Use it as an association and say so. Is a small sample always a reason to cut a study? No. It is a reason to trust a single result less, especially a large one. If the finding has been replicated, or if the study's weakness helps your argument, it can stay. Say how the sample limits it. What does the Role question add that Merit does not? Merit asks whether the study is good. Role asks whether it is useful to your argument. A strong study with no job is padding; it does not earn marks in Criteria C and D. Why is "every source agrees with me" a warning sign? Real research questions have evidence on both sides. If all your sources agree, you have probably not searched for the challenge evidence yet, and your discussion and evaluation (Criterion D) will be one-sided. When is ethics worth evaluating in a psychology EE? When it limits what the research can tell us, for example when ethical rules

items.k: Stage 4 checklist
items.x: Tick when you can Stage 4 checklist I have scored every source I plan to use with Match, Method, Merit and Role. I know what kind of claim each study's design can support. Every source I keep has a clear job in my argument. I have at least one study that challenges or qualifies my argument. I have checked whether my key studies have been replicated. My evaluation points are about specific studies, not generic. Next: Stage 5, read and take notes →

items.s: Read for what you need, note it in your own words
items.x: Aim Read for what you need, note it in your own words The IB guidance is clear: abstracts alone cannot support an EE. When you read a study, focus on the procedure and the discussion, and describe it accurately and concisely. Statistical details are rarely needed. By the end of this stage you can: read a journal article in an order that saves time record the details you need to describe and evaluate a study paraphrase properly and avoid accidental plagiarism build a literature matrix that shows how your studies compare Our example question To what extent does taking notes by hand rather than on a laptop improve students' learning from lectures?

items.s: How to read a journal article
items.k: How to read a journal article | Title and abstract | End of the introduction | Discussion | Method | Results | Two passes
items.x: Read smart How to read a journal article Title and abstract. Is it relevant? Decide whether to keep reading. Never cite from the abstract alone. End of the introduction. Find the aims and hypotheses: what exactly were they testing? Discussion. What did they conclude, how cautious were they, and what limitations do they admit? Method. Who took part, how were they allocated, and how were the key variables measured? This is where most evaluation comes from. Results. Skim for the main finding in words. You rarely need to report the statistics. Two passes First pass: steps 1 to 3, about ten minutes, to decide whether it is worth your time. Second pass: the method, slowly, with your notes template open.

items.s: What to record for every study
items.k: What to record for every study
items.x: Take notes What to record for every study Field Why you need it Full reference and DOI So you never have to find it again (APA format, see Stage 8 ) Aim To link the study to your question Sample Who, how many, how chosen: the basis for judging generalisation Design and method What claim the study can support ( Stage 4 ) How the key variables were measured The source of most specific evaluation Key findings, in words What you will report The authors' own limitations A head start on evaluation, in their words My evaluation, tagged with a concept Your own thinking, ready for Criterion D Its job in my argument Support, challenge, qualify or context ( Stage 4 ) Quotations with page numbers Only if the exact words matter. Mark them clearly as quotations Use the study notes cards to keep these in one place and download them as a literature matrix.

items.k: Paraphrase, do not patchwrite | Patchwriting | Mark quotations in your notes
items.x: Your own words Paraphrase, do not patchwrite Patchwriting means keeping the original sentence and swapping a few words. Even with a citation, it is too close to the source. A real paraphrase changes the structure and the words, keeps the meaning, and still cites the source. Read the passage until you understand it. Close it, and write the idea from memory in your own words. Check it against the original: is the meaning the same and the wording different? Add the citation. Mark quotations in your notes Most accidental plagiarism starts in notes, when copied words lose their quotation marks. Put every copied phrase in quotation marks with a page number the moment you write it down.

items.k: Build a literature matrix
items.x: See the pattern Build a literature matrix A literature matrix is a table with one row per study and one column per field. Read across a row to recall a study; read down a column to see patterns: which studies used the same measure, which samples dominate, where the findings disagree. Those patterns become your discussion. Study Sample Design Outcome measure Finding Job Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) University students Experiment Quiz soon after a short talk Laptop users more verbatim; lower conceptual scores Support Urry et al. (2021) 142 university students Direct replication Quiz soon after a short talk No significant difference in quiz scores Challenge Flanigan et al. (2024) 24 studies Meta-analysis Achievement across studies Advantage mainly when notes were reviewed Qualify Reading down the "Sample" column already shows a limitation: nearly all the evidence comes from university students.

items.k: Five quick questions
items.x: Check yourself Five quick questions Which two parts of an article does the IB guidance say to focus on? The procedure (method) and the discussion. Do you need to report t-values and p-values in your essay? Rarely. Report what was found in words and describe the method concisely and accurately. What is patchwriting? Keeping the original sentence structure and swapping a few words. It is too close to the source, even with a citation. Does a paraphrase need a citation? Yes. The idea belongs to the source, even when every word is yours. What can a literature matrix show that separate notes cannot? Patterns across studies: shared measures, dominant samples, and where findings disagree. These feed your discussion.

items.k: Stage 5 checklist
items.x: Tick when you can Stage 5 checklist I read the method and discussion of every study I use, not just the abstract. I have a complete study card for each core study. Every quotation in my notes is marked and has a page number. My paraphrases change the structure and wording, and are cited. I have a literature matrix and have looked for patterns down the columns. Next: Stage 6, build the argument →

items.s: From a pile of studies to one argument
items.k: From a pile of studies to one argument
items.x: Aim From a pile of studies to one argument Criterion C asks for a line of argument: a logical progression of ideas that begins with your question, where each point builds on the one before and leads to a well-supported conclusion. The guide also expects you to consider challenges such as counter-arguments or moderating variables. By the end of this stage you can: state a main claim that answers your question group your studies into strands that support, challenge and qualify it write a fair counter-argument and answer it check the order of your argument with a reverse outline Our example question To what extent does taking notes by hand rather than on a laptop improve students' learning from lectures?

items.k: Your main claim | Weak claim | Strong claim
items.x: Take a position Your main claim Your main claim is your answer to the question in one or two sentences. It can change as you read, and it should. Write a first version early and revise it. Weak claim "There are arguments on both sides about laptops and handwriting." Strong claim "Handwriting may give a small advantage for conceptual learning, but the effect is smaller and less reliable than first reported, and depends mainly on whether students review their notes." The strong claim takes a position, says how much ("small", "less reliable") and names a condition ("depends on review"). Each part can be argued with evidence.

items.k: Strands and a structure | Introduction | Background | Body: the case for | Body: the challenge | Body: it depends | Discussion | Conclusion | Mini-conclusions
items.x: Shape it Strands and a structure Group your studies by the job they do (from Stage 4 ), not one study per paragraph. A common shape for a psychology EE: Introduction. Context, why the question matters, key terms defined, your question, a short method paragraph (how you searched and selected studies), and where the essay is going. Background. The theory and concepts the reader needs, briefly. Body: the case for. The strongest supporting evidence, evaluated as you go. Body: the challenge. Evidence against, such as failed replications or contradictory findings. Body: it depends. Moderating variables that explain the conflict. Discussion. The evidence as a whole: recurring limitations, biases, what is still uncertain. Conclusion. A clear answer to the question that follows from everything before it. No new evidence. Mini-conclusions End each section with one sentence that says what it has shown and how it moves the argument on. It keeps you, and the examiner, on the line.

items.k: Write a counter-argument | Acknowledge | Evidence | Weaken fairly | Restate
items.x: Fair play Write a counter-argument 1 Acknowledge State the opposing view fairly, at its strongest. 2 Evidence Give the evidence for it. 3 Weaken fairly Show its limits with evidence or reasoning, not dismissal. 4 Restate Say what this means for your claim: does it survive, or does it need refining? A counter-argument that changes your claim is not a failure. It is what the IB guidance means by recognising complexity.

items.k: The reverse outline
items.x: Check the order The reverse outline Once you have a draft, write one sentence summarising each paragraph, in order. Then ask: Does every sentence connect to the research question? Does each point build on the one before? Could any two be swapped without loss? If so, the line is weak. Is any paragraph doing two jobs, or no job? Does the conclusion follow from the sentences above it?

items.k: Five quick questions
items.x: Check yourself Five quick questions What does Criterion C mean by a line of argument? A logical progression of ideas that starts from your question, where each point builds on the last and leads to a supported conclusion. Why group studies by strand rather than one study per paragraph? Strands make each paragraph do a job in the argument. One study per paragraph tends to become a list of summaries. Your counter-argument makes you change your main claim. Is that a problem? No. Refining your claim in response to evidence shows you recognise complexity, which the guide rewards. What is a moderating variable, in an EE argument? A condition the effect depends on, such as whether students review their notes. It often explains why studies disagree. What does a reverse outline check? That every paragraph links to the question, does one job, and builds on the one before, so the conclusion follows.

items.k: Stage 6 checklist
items.x: Tick when you can Stage 6 checklist I have a main claim that answers my question, with how much and when. My studies are grouped into strands with clear jobs. I have a fair counter-argument with an answer to it. I have a one-page argument map. My draft passes a reverse outline check. Next: Stage 7, write and evaluate →

items.s: Write so the argument and the evaluation are easy to see
items.x: Aim Write so the argument and the evaluation are easy to see Discussion and evaluation is the highest-weighted criterion (8 of 30 marks), and the guide expects evaluation throughout the essay. Good writing makes your argument visible: concise descriptions, specific evaluation, and wording that matches the strength of the evidence. By the end of this stage you can: write an introduction that sets up the whole essay, including a method paragraph describe a study accurately in two or three sentences evaluate inside each paragraph, tied to your question and a concept match your wording to the evidence, and stay within 4,000 words Our example question To what extent does taking notes by hand rather than on a laptop improve students' learning from lectures?

items.k: What the introduction does | Context | Key terms | The question | Method | Direction
items.x: Start well What the introduction does Context. Why does the question matter, in the real world and in psychology? Key terms. Define the variables in your question as the studies measured them. The question. State your research question exactly. Method. A short paragraph on how you searched and selected studies (from your search log, Stage 3 ). Direction. One or two sentences on how the essay will proceed. Many writers draft the introduction last, once they know what the essay actually argues.

items.s: Describe a study in two or three sentences
items.k: Describe a study in two or three sentences | Who and what | Key detail | Finding | Too much and too little | Concise and useful
items.x: Be concise Describe a study in two or three sentences The guide asks you to describe studies so that you show you understand the aim, method and findings, concisely and accurately. Detailed procedures and statistics are not needed. Who and what: [Researchers] (year) [design] [who took part] to test [aim]. Key detail: [the feature of the method your evaluation will use]. Finding: [what they found, in words]. Too much and too little "The researchers did a study where they got participants and put them in two groups and gave them a lecture and a test, and the results were t(65) = 2.10, p = .04." Concise and useful "Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) randomly assigned university students to take notes on laptops or by hand while watching short recorded talks. Laptop users copied more of the talks word for word and scored lower on conceptual, but not factual, questions."

items.k: Evaluate inside every paragraph | point | evidence | evaluation | link | Avoid the formula
items.x: Evaluate Evaluate inside every paragraph Each body paragraph can follow the same pattern: point (link to your question), evidence (the study, concisely), evaluation (a specific strength or limitation and what it means for your question), link (how far this supports your claim). Tag each evaluative sentence with one of the six concepts. If one concept never appears, ask whether it should. Bias Causality Change Measurement Perspective Responsibility Avoid the formula The IB guidance warns against discussing the same points (generalisability, ethics, gender) for every study. Evaluate what genuinely matters for each study and your question.

items.s: Match your words to the evidence
items.k: Match your words to the evidence
items.x: Hedging Match your words to the evidence Evidence Words that fit Words to avoid One experiment found, suggests, provides evidence that proves, shows conclusively Several consistent experiments or a meta-analysis strong evidence, consistently found always, beyond doubt Correlational or survey data is associated with, is linked to causes, leads to, makes Mixed findings some studies... others..., the evidence is mixed clearly, obviously Interviews and qualitative data participants described, suggests a possible reason shows that most people

items.k: Terminology traps | "Experiment" | "Reliable because it can be replicated." | "Ecological validity" | "Prove" | "Credibility"
items.x: Precise terms Terminology traps "Experiment" only for studies that manipulate an independent variable. A survey or a correlational study is not an experiment. "Reliable because it can be replicated." Replicability is not the same as reliability. Say what was replicated, and by whom. "Ecological validity" is about the setting and tasks, not the sample. For the sample, talk about generalisability or sampling bias. "Prove" almost never belongs in an EE. "Credibility" is a technical term for qualitative research, not a synonym for "believable".

items.k: Word count and presentation | Counts towards 4,000 | Does not count | Over the limit | Presentation
items.x: The rules Word count and presentation Counts towards 4,000 Introduction, body and conclusion Quotations Footnotes that explain or comment (not just reference) Does not count Title page and contents page Tables, charts and diagrams The reference list, and footnotes used only for referencing The reflective statement (written separately) Over the limit? Examiners stop reading at 4,000 words, and they do not have to read appendices. Anything essential to your argument must be in the main text. Ask your coordinator how your school counts in-text citations, and plan as if they count. Presentation: a title page, a contents page, clear headings, page numbers, one consistent referencing style, and a final check of the PDF before you upload it.

items.k: What the conclusion does
items.x: Finish well What the conclusion does Answers the research question directly, including "to what extent". Draws together the main strands and the most important limitations. Says what is still uncertain and what future research could test. Adds no new evidence.

Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) did an experiment on students at Princeton. They watched talks and took notes on laptops or by hand, and then did a test. The results were significant (p < .05). This proves that handwriting is better. However, the study was a lab experiment so it lacks ecological validity, and the sample was small and only American so it cannot be generalised. It may also be unethical because participants were not told the aim. EE-07-1 Keep your answer in your researcher's reflection space.

items.k: Five quick questions
items.x: Check yourself Five quick questions What goes in the method paragraph of a literature review? How you searched (databases, search terms) and how you selected studies (what you included and excluded, and why). Where should evaluation appear in your essay? Throughout, inside each body paragraph, not only in a final section. The guide says so explicitly. A correlational study finds laptop use is linked to lower grades. Which verb fits? "Is associated with" or "is linked to". Not "causes". Do tables and the reference list count towards 4,000 words? No. The introduction, body, conclusion, quotations and explanatory footnotes do. Can you put an important part of your argument in an appendix? No. Examiners do not have to read appendices, so anything essential must be in the main text.

items.k: Two principles | Your school decides too
items.x: Aim Two principles The IB's guidance on AI in coursework comes down to two questions. Did you use AI to help you learn? That is fine. Did you use AI to pretend you did something you did not? That is not. By the end of this stage you can: sort common uses of AI into acceptable, ask first, and not acceptable acknowledge any AI use in the way the IB expects check every reference yourself, because AI tools invent convincing ones reference in APA 7, and use an AI prompt that checks your formatting without touching your writing Your school decides too The IB says there are no hard rules and leaves room for teachers' judgement. Your school's AI policy and your supervisor can be stricter than this page. When in doubt, ask before you use a tool, not after. Based on the IB's guidance on evaluating AI use in student coursework (2024) and annex 6 of the IB academic integrity policy, paraphrased.

items.s: What is and is not acceptable
items.k: What is and is not acceptable | Green | Amber | Red
items.x: Green, amber, red What is and is not acceptable Green Acceptable. Acknowledge it. Amber Depends on context. Ask your supervisor first. Red Not acceptable in your EE. Light Use IB scenario Green Ask for the main ideas and possible sources, then find and read every source yourself 1 Green Ask for counter-arguments, then search for studies that test them 2 Green Ask for spelling and grammar suggestions (not a rewrite), keep your original, and tell your supervisor 9 Green Ask for a structure template, fill it in yourself, and acknowledge the tool 13 Amber Ask for a sample paragraph to learn what one looks like, then write your own from scratch 6 Amber Ask AI to mark or give feedback on your essay. The IB discourages this for assessed work, because your supervisor gives the feedback 10 Red Ask AI to write a whole model essay on your question, even to rewrite in your own words 5 Red Paste quotations AI gave you without reading the source, even if referenced 3 Red Ask AI to write your research question 4 Red Ask AI to rewrite your essay, or to translate it for submission 7, 8 Red Use an AI-written reflection 11 Red Hide that you used AI, even if the use itself was acceptable 12 Practise

items.k: Five rules for your EE | Check every reference yourself | Mark and reference AI text | Keep your trail | Write an AI use statement | The reflection is yours alone
items.x: The rules Five rules for your EE Check every reference yourself. AI tools invent references that look real, or attach a real DOI to a paper that does not exist. Open each source before it goes in your essay. Mark and reference AI text. If you copy or paraphrase anything an AI tool produced, put it in quotation marks and reference the tool, with the prompt you gave it and the date, in your school's referencing style. Keep your trail. Keep your drafts, notes and AI chat history. Your supervisor may ask to see them or to talk with you about your essay. Write an AI use statement. Add a short statement at the end of your work describing how you used AI, even for uses that need no reference. The reflection is yours alone. No AI tool can tell the story of your own learning. Why not just ask AI to "improve the structure"? Some EE guides suggest it. We do not, because improving the structure of an argument is improving the argument, and the argument must be yours. The IB treats a rewrite that improves the coherence of your argument as a wholesale rewrite.

items.k: How to acknowledge AI
items.x: Be open How to acknowledge AI The IB's focus is transparency, not perfect formatting: a reader must be able to see what is yours and what is not. There are three places AI use can appear. Where When Pattern In the text You quote or paraphrase AI output When prompted with "[your prompt]" on [date], [Tool] suggested "[words you quote]" ([Company], [year]). In the reference list Whenever you cite it in the text [Company]. ([Year]). [Tool name] ([version]) [Large language model]. [URL] AI use statement Always, after the end of your essay "I used [tool] on [dates] to [purpose]. I checked everything it suggested against the original sources, and all analysis and wording in this essay are my own." The acknowledgement builder fills these in for you.

items.s: Check a reference in two minutes
items.k: Check a reference in two minutes | Open the DOI | Search the exact title | Match every detail | Read it
items.x: Check before you cite Check a reference in two minutes Open the DOI. Type https://doi.org/ followed by the DOI. Does it open, and is it the same paper? Search the exact title in quotation marks in Google Scholar. A real paper almost always appears. Match every detail: authors and their order, year, journal, volume, issue and pages. Read it. Make sure the paper says what you claim it says. Be ready to explain any source at your viva.

items.k: Why APA 7 | in-text citation | reference list
items.x: One style Why APA 7 The IB does not require a particular style. It requires that you reference consistently, in a way that lets a reader find every source. Psychology uses APA (7th edition), so that is the style for your EE. APA has two parts that must match: a short in-text citation every time you use a source, and a full entry in the reference list at the end. Every citation needs an entry, and every entry needs at least one citation.

items.k: In-text citations
items.x: In the text In-text citations Case In brackets In the sentence One author (Kiewra, 1989) Kiewra (1989) argued... Two authors (Mueller & Oppenheimer, 2014) Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) found... Three or more (Morehead et al., 2019) Morehead et al. (2019) found... Group author First time: (World Health Organization [WHO], 2017). Then: (WHO, 2017) The World Health Organization (WHO, 2017) reported... Direct quotation (Author, year, p. 12) Author (year) wrote that "..." (p. 12). Two or more works (Morehead et al., 2019; Urry et al., 2021) Alphabetical order, separated by semicolons A source you only read about (Original author, year, as cited in Author you read, year) Only list the source you actually read. Better: find and read the original. Use "&" inside brackets and "and" in the sentence. "Et al." is used from the first citation when there are three or more authors.

items.k: The reference list | References | hanging indent | sentence case | Templates
items.x: At the end The reference list Title it References . Put entries in alphabetical order by the first author's surname. Use a hanging indent : the first line of each entry starts at the margin and the rest are indented. Write surnames, then initials. Keep the authors in the order the article gives. List up to 20 authors; for 21 or more, list the first 19, then ". . .", then the last author. Article and book titles use sentence case : capitals only for the first word, the first word after a colon, and names. Journal names use capitals for main words. The journal name and the volume number are in italics ; the issue number in brackets is not. Write the DOI as a link: https://doi.org/... . No full stop after a DOI or URL. Templates Type Pattern Journal article Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). Title of the article: Subtitle in sentence case. Journal Name , volume (issue), first page–last page. https://doi.org/xxxx Book Author, A. A. (Year). Title of the book: Subtitle in sentence case (2nd ed.). Publisher. Chapter in an edited book Author, A. A. (Year). Title of the chapter. In E. E. Editor (Ed.), Title of the book (pp. xx–xx). Publisher. Report by an organisation Organisation

items.k: Five quick questions
items.x: Check yourself Five quick questions An AI tool gives you a reference with a working DOI. Is that enough to cite it? No. A common AI mistake is attaching a real DOI to an invented paper. Check that the DOI opens the same paper, with the same authors, year and title, and read the paper before you cite it. You used AI only to suggest search terms. Do you need to mention it? Yes, in your AI use statement. It needs no in-text citation because no AI text appears in your essay, but hiding any AI use is not acceptable. Why is asking AI to rewrite your essay "so it flows better" not acceptable? A rewrite changes who wrote the essay. If it improves the coherence of your argument, the IB treats it as a wholesale rewrite. What three things does the IB expect when you quote AI output? Quotation marks, a reference to the tool in your school's style, and the prompt you gave it with the date. How do you cite a paper with three authors in APA 7? First author's surname, "et al.", year, from the very first citation: (Morehead et al., 2019). In the reference list, all three authors are listed in full.

items.k: The viva voce
items.x: The final session The viva voce The viva voce is a short concluding interview with your supervisor after you have handed in your final essay. It is a chance to talk about what you learned, and it also helps your supervisor confirm the work is your own. Your essay is not changed after the viva. Reread your essay and your researcher's reflection space the day before. Be ready to explain any study in your essay in your own words, without notes. Think of a real problem you hit and how you solved it, and a moment your thinking changed. Practise with the mock viva .

Describes (earns little) Evaluates (earns more) "I met my supervisor three times and changed my question."
